META.subtitleDoc: CBE Phenomenon-Driven Lesson Sequence — Sub-Strand 2.3 (8 Lessons)

UNIT.subject: Essential Mathematics
UNIT.content:
• Identification of sides of a right-angled triangle (hypotenuse, opposite, adjacent) relative to a specific acute angle
• Sine, cosine and tangent ratios of acute angles in a right-angled triangle
• Sines and cosines of complementary angles and their relationship
• Application of trigonometric ratios to angles of elevation
• Application of trigonometric ratios to angles of depression
• Construction and use of a simple clinometer to measure angles of elevation and depression
• Use of trigonometric tables and digital tools to find trigonometric ratios
• Real-life applications of trigonometry in the immediate environment
UNIT.learningOutcomes:
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) identify the sides of a right-angled triangle in relation to a particular angle,
b) determine the sine, cosine and tangent of acute angles in a right-angled triangle,
c) relate sines and cosines of complementary angles,
d) apply trigonometric ratios to angles of elevation and depression,
e) recognise the use of trigonometry in real-life situations.
UNIT.coreCompetencies:
• Self-efficacy: The learner makes observations and establishes the relationships between the sine and cosine ratios of complementary angles, building confidence in their own mathematical reasoning as they generate and verify the pattern independently.
• Learning to learn: The learner learns collaboratively while constructing a simple clinometer using locally available materials (cardboard, straw, string, protractor) and using it as a hands-on learning resource for measuring angles of elevation and depression in the school environment.
UNIT.values:
• Love: The learner demonstrates a caring attitude towards others when using a simple clinometer to measure the angle of elevation and depression of different objects in the immediate environment, ensuring every group member has a turn and that measurements are taken safely and considerately.
• Responsibility: The learner takes care of instruments such as rulers, geometrical sets, graph paper and digital devices used during trigonometry activities, returning them in good condition and ensuring shared resources are available for peers.
UNIT.sep:
• Asking Questions and Defining Problems: Learners articulate what information is needed (angle, known side) to find an unknown height or distance, framing trigonometry as a tool for answering real measurement questions about their environment.
• Planning and Carrying Out Investigations: Learners design and carry out a clinometer investigation — identifying objects to measure, deciding on measurement positions, recording angle and distance data, and checking results for consistency.
• Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking: Learners select and apply the appropriate trigonometric ratio (sin, cos, tan) to compute unknown sides and angles, evaluate answers for reasonableness, and use digital tools (calculators, online resources) to verify computations.
• Constructing Explanations: Learners use their generated table of complementary angles and their sine/cosine values to construct a reasoned explanation for why sin θ = cos(90° − θ), connecting numerical patterns to geometric reasoning.
• Obtaining, Evaluating and Communicating Information: Learners present clinometer findings and trigonometric solutions to peers, critique each other's methods, and evaluate the accuracy of real-world measurements against calculated values.
UNIT.pcis:
• Self-esteem: The learners acquire and strengthen self-esteem while designing and making a simple clinometer using locally available materials (cardboard, string, protractor, drinking straw) and successfully using it as a functional learning resource for measuring real angles in their school environment.
• Life Skills (Critical Thinking and Problem Solving): Learners apply trigonometric ratios to authentic measurement problems — such as estimating the height of a flagpole, water tank, or school building in Nairobi — developing analytical and decision-making skills transferable to daily life.
• Education for Sustainable Development: Learners use locally sourced, low-cost materials to construct the clinometer, reinforcing resourcefulness and environmental awareness while achieving a meaningful mathematical learning outcome.
UNIT.careers:
• Surveying and Land Management: Trigonometric ratios are foundational tools for surveyors who map land parcels across Kenya's counties — from the Rift Valley to the Coast — measuring distances and elevations using clinometers and theodolites.
• Architecture and Building Construction: Architects and construction engineers in Kenya use angles of elevation, roof pitch calculations and trigonometric ratios when designing and constructing buildings, ensuring structural stability.
• Aviation and Navigation: Pilots and navigators at airports such as JKIA (Nairobi) and Moi International Airport (Mombasa) apply trigonometry to calculate flight approach angles, altitudes and distances.
• Sports Coaching and Biomechanics: Sports scientists and coaches working with Kenyan athletes (e.g., track and field at Kipchoge Keino Stadium, Eldoret) use angle analysis to optimise throwing, jumping and running techniques.
• Photography and Media Technology: Photographers and videographers computing camera angles, framing shots and calculating perspective use principles directly related to trigonometric ratios.
• Forestry and Environmental Science: Forest officers in Kenya's Aberdare and Mau Forest complexes use clinometers to measure tree heights and terrain slopes — a direct application of angles of elevation.
UNIT.focus: This unit introduces learners to trigonometry through a practical, investigation-led approach anchored in the Kenyan built and natural environment. Learners move from identifying the sides of a right-angled triangle, through deriving and applying the three trigonometric ratios, to discovering the complementary-angle relationship and finally deploying their knowledge to solve real problems involving angles of elevation and depression using a student-built clinometer. Throughout the 8 lessons, every concept is connected back to the anchoring phenomenon of estimating the height of an inaccessible structure using only a measured distance and an angle, reinforcing trigonometry as a practical, empowering tool rather than an abstract set of rules.
UNIT.phenomenon:
ANCHORING PHENOMENON — "How tall is the water tank without climbing it?"

At many Kenyan schools and homesteads, a large elevated water tank (sometimes mounted on a steel frame 4–8 metres high) is a familiar sight. Students can clearly see the tank from the ground but cannot climb it or use a tape measure along its height directly.

The teacher presents this puzzling scenario: Two students stand at different positions on the ground, both a known horizontal distance from the base of the water-tank tower. Each student uses a simple angle-measuring device (a protractor and string) to sight the top of the tank and records a different angle. Without any additional climbing or measuring, can we use ONLY these two pieces of information — the horizontal distance and the measured angle — to calculate exactly how high the top of the tank is above the ground?

This is puzzling because:
(1) The students never measured the height directly, yet they can calculate it precisely.
(2) Two students at different distances get different angles but should arrive at the SAME height — a powerful consistency check.
(3) The same method, scaled up, is how surveyors map the Kenyan highlands, how engineers design the Thika Superhighway overpasses, and how foresters in the Mau Forest measure tree heights without felling them.

The phenomenon is revisited and refined in every lesson: learners begin unable to explain it, gradually acquire the ratio tools (sin, cos, tan), discover the complementary-angle shortcut, build their own clinometer, and in the final lesson use the clinometer outdoors to measure a real structure and confirm their prediction — closing the explanatory loop completely.
UNIT.supportingPhenomena:
• THE LEANING SIGN BOARD: A rectangular signboard on a tilted pole outside the school gate — learners notice the pole makes an acute angle with the ground. How do we find the actual height the sign reaches without measuring along the pole? (Supports: identifying opposite/adjacent/hypotenuse and setting up a tan ratio.)
• THE SHADOW PUZZLE: At midday, a vertical maize stalk in the school garden casts a short shadow; in the late afternoon the same stalk casts a much longer shadow. Why does the shadow length change, and can we use the shadow to find the height of the stalk? (Supports: angle of elevation of the sun, tan ratio, and the idea that the same height gives different ratios at different angles.)
• THE MIRROR ON THE FLOOR: A small mirror is placed flat on the ground between a learner and the base of a wall. The learner steps back until they can just see the top of the wall in the mirror. The triangle formed is similar to the wall triangle. How is this related to the ratios we computed? (Supports: connecting similar triangles to constant trigonometric ratios.)
• THE STAIRCASE RAMP: A newly built concrete ramp at a Nairobi hospital rises 1.2 m over a horizontal run of 4.8 m. Is this ramp accessible for wheelchair users (angle < 14°)? (Supports: applying arctan/inverse trigonometry and angles of elevation in a real accessibility-design context.)
UNIT.drivingQuestion:
DRIVING QUESTION: How can we use the angles and one side of a right-angled triangle to find any unknown height or distance in our environment — without ever measuring it directly?

KICD KEY INQUIRY QUESTION:
1. Why is trigonometry important?
UNIT.storylineThread:
Lesson 1 — PREDICT: "The Water Tank Problem" (Anchoring Phenomenon Launch)
Learners observe a photograph/diagram of the school water tank or a similar elevated structure. In small groups they predict: "What information would you need, and how would you use it, to find the height of the tank without climbing?" Groups record predictions on sticky notes for the Driving Question Board (DQB). Teacher introduces vocabulary: right-angled triangle, hypotenuse, opposite side, adjacent side. Learners physically identify these sides in right-angled shapes around the classroom (door frames, window corners, book corners) with reference to a named acute angle. DQB is set up with the driving question posted prominently.

Lesson 2 — OBSERVE (Part 1): Deriving the Three Trigonometric Ratios
Learners use rulers and protractors to draw three different right-angled triangles each with the same acute angle (e.g., 35°) but different sizes. They measure the opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse for each triangle and compute the three ratios (opp/hyp, adj/hyp, opp/adj) in a table. Learners notice each ratio remains constant regardless of triangle size — a key discovery. Teacher names the ratios: sine, cosine, tangent. Learners use a scientific calculator to verify their measured ratios against calculator values. Connection to phenomenon: "These constant ratios are exactly what let us calculate the tank height from any distance!"

Lesson 3 — OBSERVE (Part 2): Sine and Cosine of Complementary Angles
Learners generate a table of angle pairs that sum to 90° (e.g., 20° & 70°, 35° & 55°, 45° & 45°) and record their sines and cosines. They discover that sin θ = cos(90° − θ) and cos θ = sin(90° − θ). Learners construct an explanation for this pattern using a right-angled triangle diagram, noting that the "opposite" for one angle is the "adjacent" for its complement. DQB is updated: new understanding posted, new questions raised (e.g., "Does this work for ALL angles?").

Lesson 4 — EXPLAIN (Part 1): Applying Trigonometric Ratios to Find Unknown Sides
Guided practice: learners use sin, cos and tan to calculate unknown sides in right-angled triangles drawn on graph paper. Problems are set in Kenyan contexts — length of a roof rafter in Kisumu, distance across a stream in Kericho, height of a mango tree in a Mombasa compound. Learners practise selecting the correct ratio, setting up the equation and solving. Peer checking of answers. Connection to phenomenon: learners set up and solve the water-tank calculation for the first time using a given angle and distance.

Lesson 5 — OBSERVE (Part 3): Angle of Elevation — Clinometer Construction (Project Lesson)
Learners construct a simple clinometer using a cardboard protractor, drinking straw, string and a small weight (stone or metal washer). Teacher models how to sight along the straw to an elevated object and read the angle of elevation. Learners practise sighting objects of known approximate height in the classroom. Discussion: what is the "angle of elevation"? How does it relate to the right-angled triangle? DQB updated with new vocabulary and connections.

Lesson 6 — OBSERVE (Part 4): Angle of Depression and Outdoor Measurement
Learners take their clinometers outdoors. Working in groups of 3–4, they measure the angle of elevation to the top of the school flagpole, water tank, or a tall tree, and record the horizontal distance from the base. They also identify and measure an angle of depression (e.g., sighting from a raised veranda down to a ground-level marker). Data is recorded on structured worksheets. Back in the classroom, each group calculates the height of the object using the appropriate trigonometric ratio. Groups compare results and discuss sources of error.

Lesson 7 — EXPLAIN (Part 2): Problem Solving — Angles of Elevation and Depression
Structured problem-solving lesson using multi-step real-life scenarios: a Rift Valley farmer estimating the height of a cliff face, a diver at Watamu estimating depth from a boat, a construction worker in Nairobi checking the angle of a ramp. Learners work individually then compare with a partner. Common errors (confusing opposite/adjacent, not identifying the correct reference angle) are addressed explicitly. DQB is updated: learners move sticky notes from "questions" to "answered" and add new refined understandings. Learners revisit their original predictions from Lesson 1 and evaluate them.

Lesson 8 — MODEL BUILDING & SUMMATIVE CLOSURE: "Solving the Water Tank Problem"
Learners use all accumulated knowledge to produce a final written and diagrammatic solution to the original anchoring phenomenon. Each learner draws a labelled diagram of the water-tank scenario, identifies the right-angled triangle, selects and applies the correct trigonometric ratio, calculates the height, and writes a clear explanation of their method. Groups present their clinometer project findings (angle, distance, calculated height, reflection on accuracy). Teacher facilitates a whole-class DQB review — all original questions are revisited and either answered or identified as leading to future learning (e.g., trigonometry of non-right-angled triangles). Formative assessment via class activity and portfolio entry.

LESSONS.title: The Water Tank Problem: Predict and Name the Sides
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (1 lesson); extend to a double lesson if the side-naming practice is not finished
LESSONS.aresKeywords: right-angled triangle, hypotenuse, opposite side, adjacent side, angle θ (theta), angle of elevation, clinometer, Driving Question Board, prediction

slo.purpose: To launch the anchoring phenomenon (how tall is the Kilimani Secondary School water tank without climbing it?), to record learners' own predictions about how it might be done, and to give learners the vocabulary they need to name the hypotenuse, opposite and adjacent sides of a right-angled triangle relative to a chosen acute angle θ.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (a) identify the right-angled triangle in relation to a particular angle, naming the hypotenuse, the opposite side and the adjacent side (KICD Specific Learning Outcome 2.3 a); (b) explain that the names opposite and adjacent change when the chosen angle changes, while the hypotenuse does not; (c) describe the tank problem as a right-angled triangle made by the tower, the ground and the line of sight.
slo.skills: NGSS-aligned practices: Asking Questions and Defining Problems (learners write questions for the Driving Question Board); Developing and Using Models (learners draw an initial model of the tank, ground and line of sight); Constructing Explanations (learners give a reasoned prediction). Mathematical processes: reasoning, communication, connection and collaboration. Core competencies: Self-efficacy (the learner makes observations and establishes relationships) and Learning to learn (the learner learns collaboratively).
slo.attitudes: Love: the learner demonstrates a caring attitude to others by listening and taking turns when working in pairs and sharing predictions. Self-esteem (PCI): the learner feels confident that every prediction is valued at the start of a new topic. Curiosity and appreciation of how mathematics is used in real life.
slo.keyInquiry: Why is trigonometry important? (KICD Key Inquiry Question). Driving question: How can we use the angles and one side of a right-angled triangle to find any unknown height or distance in our environment, without ever measuring it directly?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the PREDICT lesson of the unit. Learners meet the water tank problem, make predictions without any new formula, and gain the side-naming language that Lesson 2 uses to build sine, cosine and tangent. The predictions and the Driving Question Board (DQB) created today are revisited in Lesson 7 (evaluating the predictions) and answered fully in Lesson 8. No numbers for the tank are given today and the tank's height is not revealed.
slo.safetyNotes: This lesson is carried out entirely indoors or at the classroom door, and nobody is to climb the tank, its steel frame or any structure. If the class looks out at the tank tower, they stay on level ground, keep away from the tower base and do not look directly at the sun. Use blunt-ended pencils and keep rulers and protractors on the desks. Reinforce the message that the whole point of trigonometry is to measure things safely, without climbing.

LESSONS.overview: Madam Achieng opens the lesson by describing the steel-framed water tank tower at Kilimani Secondary School in Nakuru. Everyone can see the tank but nobody may climb it, and a tape cannot be run up it from the ground. Two Grade 10 learners, Wanjiru and Otieno, stand at different distances from the base of the tower. Each sights the top of the tank with a simple protractor-and-string angle-measuring device, and they record different angles because they stand at different distances. Learners predict, individually and then in pairs, whether the height of the tank can be found from only a horizontal distance and an angle, and whether both learners should get the same answer. No numbers are given today. Learners sketch a first model of the situation and see that it forms a right-angled triangle, using what they already know from Grade 9 about right-angled triangles and Pythagoras. They then learn to name the hypotenuse, opposite and adjacent sides relative to a chosen angle θ, practising with the triangle of the tank, a door frame and a roof truss. Finally they open the Driving Question Board (DQB) with questions from their own wondering. The DQB has the columns Questions, Answered and New understandings.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners look at a large sketch or a view from the window of the water tank tower at Kilimani Secondary School. They hear the story: Wanjiru stands near the tower and sights the top of the tank with a protractor and string, and Otieno stands further back and does the same. They are told that the two learners record different angles, and that no numbers are being given yet. On a sheet or in their exercise books, learners individually write: (1) How could we find the height of the top of the tank without climbing it or hanging a tape down from it? (2) Wanjiru is closer than Otieno. Who do you think records the larger angle? (3) Will Wanjiru and Otieno calculate the same height or different heights? Why? They then sketch a quick picture of the tank, the ground and the line of sight. Then they share their ideas with a partner and as a class. Learners may predict things such as 'use the shadow' or 'draw a scale diagram', which are welcome.
framework.teacherMoves: Madam Achieng says: "Look out of the window at our tank tower. Nobody is allowed to climb it. Today's problem is: how tall is the top of the tank, without climbing it?" She describes Wanjiru and Otieno and the two different angles, drawing a simple diagram on the board with two stick figures at different distances but no numbers. She says: "I will not tell you the answer or any formula today. I want your honest prediction." Then she gives 2 minutes of silent individual writing time. After the writing she gives WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before calling on anyone. She cold-calls 3 learners with: "Tell us your prediction and one reason." Then she takes a quick show of hands: "Who thinks Wanjiru gets the larger angle? Who thinks Otieno?" and records the counts on the board. She also asks, "Who thinks they will get the same height? Different?" She records the counts without judging them as right or wrong and keeps all the written predictions to revisit in Lesson 7.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction with reasoning (Predict-Share-Revisit): writing a prediction and a reason commits learners to an idea, so they notice later when the evidence changes or confirms it. The class tally makes the disagreement about the larger angle and the same height visible, and creates a genuine need to know. It also surfaces preconceptions, such as thinking that the learner standing further away should see a larger angle.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether each learner writes a prediction with a reason and not just 'I don't know'. Indicators: at least 80 percent of learners have written an answer to all three questions; sketches show the tank, the ground and a sight line; the count of learners predicting the same height versus different heights is recorded. Note names of learners with misconceptions (for example, 'the farther learner gets a bigger angle') for follow-up in Lessons 2 and 5.

framework.learnerExperience: In pairs, learners examine a labelled diagram of the tank problem prepared by the teacher on the board or on a printed sheet. It shows a vertical tower, level ground, a horizontal line from the learner to the base of the tower, and a line of sight from the learner's eye to the top of the tank, with the angle of elevation marked at the learner's eye. They notice that the three lines form a right-angled triangle, with the right angle at the base of the tower. They recall Grade 9 knowledge: the triangle has a right angle, and Pythagoras' theorem links the three sides. They then look at the same triangle from two different learners' positions (Wanjiru's and Otieno's) and see two triangles with the same vertical side but different horizontal sides and different angles. Learners also look at other right-angled triangles in the classroom: a door frame, a window frame, a roof truss seen through the doorway, and a set square, to see right-angled triangles in their own surroundings.
framework.teacherMoves: Madam Achieng says: "Look carefully. What shapes can you see in this picture? Talk to your partner for one minute." She gives WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after the pair talk, then cold-calls 2 pairs: "What shape did you find, and where is the right angle?" She then asks, "What do you remember from Grade 9 about right-angled triangles and Pythagoras?" and cold-calls 2 learners, recording on the board that a² + b² = c² connects the three sides, with the longest side opposite the right angle. She points out that Pythagoras needs two sides to find the third, but here the unknown is a height and the information is an angle and a distance. She says: "Pythagoras alone cannot help us yet. We have an angle. What else do we need?" She holds back from naming sine, cosine or tangent, because that is for Lesson 2. She then walks around and asks pairs, "Where else in this room can you find a right-angled triangle?"
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Noticing and Wondering with a model diagram: a labelled picture lets every learner look for structure before any new terms are given. Connecting to prior knowledge (Grade 9 right-angled triangles and Pythagoras) lets learners see what they already can and cannot do, which makes the gap, using an angle to find a side, clear and motivates the unit.
framework.formativeAssessment: Listen for pairs who can identify the right angle at the base of the tower and describe the triangle as made by the tower, the ground and the line of sight. Indicators: learners correctly state that the longest side is opposite the right angle; at least 3 pairs name an example of a right-angled triangle in the room; learners state that Pythagoras needs two sides but the situation gives a distance and an angle. Note pairs who do not recognise the right angle and give them a set square to check.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners now learn how to name the sides of a right-angled triangle relative to a chosen acute angle θ (theta). Madam Achieng marks the angle of elevation at Wanjiru's eye as θ. With the class, they name: the hypotenuse (the side opposite the right angle, always the longest), the opposite side (across from θ, which in the tank problem is the vertical side up the tower), and the adjacent side (next to θ but not the hypotenuse, which here is the horizontal distance along the ground). In pairs, learners label printed or board triangles, such as a door-frame triangle, a roof truss triangle and a ramp triangle. They then do the key step: the angle is moved to the other acute angle of the same triangle, and learners discover that opposite and adjacent swap, while the hypotenuse stays the same. They practise with at least four triangles, labelling the three sides for the angle marked θ each time, and explain the reason for each label to a partner.
framework.teacherMoves: Madam Achieng says: "We need a shared language. Let's call the acute angle we are interested in θ, pronounced theta." She draws the tank triangle and models: "First find the right angle. The side across from it is the hypotenuse. Next, stand at θ and ask: which side is across from me? That is the opposite. The side that is next to me, and is not the hypotenuse, is the adjacent." She uses the same colour for each side name on every diagram. She asks, "In our tank triangle, which side is the height of the tank above eye level? Which is the distance Wanjiru stands from the tower?" and gives WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-calls 3 learners. She then moves the angle to the top vertex and asks: "Now θ is here. Which side is opposite now? Which is adjacent?" She cold-calls 2 pairs. She gives each pair 4 triangles in different orientations (including one turned upside down so learners do not rely on position) to label, and circulates asking, "How do you know that is the opposite side?" She does not introduce sin, cos or tan; if a learner asks, she says: "Good question. Keep it on the board for our next lesson." She then returns to the phenomenon: "For Wanjiru and Otieno, the height is the opposite side and the distance is the adjacent. Their angles are different. Why might that matter?"
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Modelling then guided practice with a contrasting case: moving the angle in the same triangle shows that the names depend on the chosen angle, which prevents the common misconception that opposite and adjacent are fixed labels. Using varied orientations breaks the habit of reading 'opposite' as 'on the other side of the page'. Re-tying the labels to the tank connects the vocabulary to the phenomenon, so the terms have a purpose.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check the labelled triangles. Success indicators: learners correctly label the hypotenuse in all 4 triangles (including the rotated one); at least 75 percent label opposite and adjacent correctly for the marked θ; learners can explain 'the hypotenuse stays the same but opposite and adjacent swap when we move θ'. Common errors to look out for: calling the vertical side 'opposite' regardless of θ; calling the longest-looking side the hypotenuse instead of the one across from the right angle. Ask learners making these errors, 'Point to the right angle first, then to θ.' Give a quick exit ticket with one triangle to label.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners open the class Driving Question Board. Madam Achieng writes the Driving Question at the top: 'How can we use the angles and one side of a right-angled triangle to find any unknown height or distance in our environment, without ever measuring it directly?' and draws three columns: Questions, Answered and New understandings. Individually, learners write at least two questions on sticky notes or pieces of paper about the tank problem and the tools they might need (for example: Why do Wanjiru and Otieno get different angles? How can an angle help us find a height? Can we get the same answer from two places? How do surveyors in the Kenyan highlands do this? How do engineers on the Thika Superhighway use it? How do foresters in the Mau Forest measure trees?). Then in groups of four they sort their questions into themes (angles, the instrument, the method, the real world), choose their best one and stick it on the board under Questions. The class also adds today's learning, 'We can name hypotenuse, opposite and adjacent', to the New understandings column.
framework.teacherMoves: Madam Achieng says: "Scientists and surveyors begin with questions. What are you still wondering about the tank?" She gives 2 minutes of silent writing time, then 3 minutes of group sorting. She gives WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before asking for volunteers, then cold-calls 4 groups to read their chosen question aloud and say why it matters. She places each question on the DQB under a theme heading, grouping similar ones. She says: "Which of these can we start answering today? Which need more tools?" She moves 'What are opposite and adjacent sides?' into Answered, with a short note, and adds 'Side names depend on θ' under New understandings. She promises: "We will return to this board in every lesson." She points out the links between questions: for example, 'Why do different distances give different angles?' will be linked to Lessons 2 and 5. She leaves the board visible or photographs it for later lessons.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board: learners' own questions create ownership and a map of the unit. Sorting questions into themes helps learners see the structure of what they need to learn, and the Answered and New understandings columns give a visible record of growing understanding that the class returns to in every lesson.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look at the quality of questions. Indicators: each learner has written at least 2 questions; at least half of the groups have a question that is linked to the mathematics (angle, distance, height, ratio) and not just a factual question; at least 1 question is about why the same height should come from different angles. Learners whose questions are only 'What is the answer?' should be asked, 'What would you need to know to work it out?' Keep a list of unanswered questions to guide the next lessons.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners draw an Initial Model in their exercise books, titled 'How can we find the height of the tank without climbing it?' The model includes: a labelled sketch of the tank tower, the ground, and Wanjiru's position; the line of sight to the top of the tank; a right-angled triangle drawn on the sketch with θ marked at the learner's eye and the three sides labelled hypotenuse, opposite and adjacent; a second position for Otieno further from the tower with its own angle marked; and a written sentence for their current idea: 'I think we can find the height by ...'. A short box beneath says 'What I am still not sure about'. They share the model with a partner and add one improvement based on the partner's comments. The model stays in their books and is revised in each lesson, with the final version completed in Lesson 8.
framework.teacherMoves: Madam Achieng says: "Draw your first model of the tank problem. Show the tower, the ground, the line of sight and the right-angled triangle. Label the sides for the angle θ at the learner's eye." She allows 6 minutes. She circulates and asks: "Where is the hypotenuse in your picture? What is the opposite side for the angle you marked?" She gives WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question. She then cold-calls 3 learners to explain their models and chooses one model to display. For the exit ticket she asks learners to write one sentence: 'The side that stands for the height of the tank above eye level is the _____ side.' She then closes: "Next lesson we will see whether the ratio of the sides changes when the triangle gets bigger or smaller while the angle stays the same. Keep your predictions safe. We will test them." She collects the exit tickets.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Initial model building: drawing a model before instruction records current thinking and shows learners that models are revised as evidence comes in. Including the labelled triangle and two positions turns the phenomenon into a mathematical structure, ready for the ratios in Lesson 2. The 'still not sure' box encourages honest uncertainty.
framework.formativeAssessment: Review models and exit tickets. Indicators: the model shows a right-angled triangle with the right angle at the base of the tower; the vertical side to the top of the tank is labelled opposite and the ground distance is labelled adjacent relative to θ at the eye; two different positions are shown with different angles; the exit ticket answer is 'opposite'. Learners who label incorrectly are to be reminded to start with the right angle and then θ, and re-checked at the start of Lesson 2.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: (1) Did learners make real predictions about the tank, and what proportion predicted that Wanjiru and Otieno would get the same height? Keep the tally for Lesson 7. (2) Which side-naming errors were most common (for example, calling the vertical side always opposite, or mislabelling the hypotenuse when the triangle was rotated)? Plan quick re-practice at the start of Lesson 2. (3) Were the DQB questions about the mathematics, and which questions can be connected directly to Lessons 2 to 8? (4) Did every learner, including quieter ones, take part in sharing predictions? (5) Did you resist naming sine, cosine and tangent today? Note any learners who already know the terms and could help others in Lesson 2. (6) Is the DQB placed where learners can see it, and are the sticky notes secure? Note changes for the next lesson.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that the water tank tower at Kilimani Secondary School cannot be climbed, yet Wanjiru and Otieno stand at different distances from its base and sight the top of the tank to record different angles. The tower, the ground and the line of sight form a right-angled triangle.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned to name the sides of a right-angled triangle relative to a chosen acute angle θ: the hypotenuse is opposite the right angle and is the longest side; the opposite side is across from θ; the adjacent side is next to θ but is not the hypotenuse. When θ moves to the other acute angle, opposite and adjacent swap but the hypotenuse stays the same.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We can say that the height of the tank above eye level is the opposite side and the distance from the learner to the tower is the adjacent side for the angle at the learner's eye, but we cannot yet explain how the angle and distance give the height, or whether Wanjiru and Otieno should get the same answer. These questions are on our Driving Question Board and we will answer them in the next lessons.

LESSONS.title: Deriving sine, cosine and tangent: Why does the tank method work at any distance?
LESSONS.aresKeywords: sine, cosine, tangent, ratio, constant ratio, similar triangles, opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse, 35°, calculator DEG mode, water tank, Kilimani Secondary School

slo.purpose: Learners discover that for a fixed angle the ratios of the sides of a right-angled triangle stay the same however big the triangle is, and name these ratios sine, cosine and tangent. This explains why Wanjiru and Otieno can stand at different distances and still find the tank height.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: a) identify the right-angled triangle in relation to a particular angle; b) determine the sine, cosine and tangent of acute angles in a right-angled triangle. Definitions: sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse, tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent.
slo.skills: Measuring lengths to the nearest 0.1 cm; calculating ratios to 3 decimal places; analysing and interpreting data (NGSS SEP: Analyzing and Interpreting Data); looking for patterns and constructing explanations from evidence; using a calculator in DEG mode.
slo.attitudes: Core competency, Self-efficacy: the learner makes observations and establishes relationships between the ratios. Value, Love: the learner shows care for peers by sharing measuring tools and checking each other's work. Appreciate the use of trigonometry in real-life situations. PCI, Self-esteem: learners gain confidence by discovering a rule themselves from their own data.
slo.keyInquiry: Why is trigonometry important? (KICD) Lesson question: Why do Wanjiru, at 8 m, and Otieno, at 10 m, get different angles but the same tank height, and what is it about a triangle that stays the same?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 launched the tank problem and named the sides opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse. Lesson 2 supplies the key idea behind the method: for a fixed angle the side ratios do not depend on triangle size, so they can be named (sin, cos, tan) and read from a calculator. Later lessons use this to find unknown sides, discover the complementary-angle link and build the clinometer.
slo.safetyNotes: Sharp pencils and compass points: carry them point-down and do not point them at others. Use rulers sensibly, not as swords. Keep the walkway clear when groups move to the DQB. Learners share one calculator per pair and handle it carefully.

LESSONS.overview: Madam Achieng opens by recalling the Kilimani Secondary School tank tower from Lesson 1: Wanjiru stands 8 m away and reads a bigger angle than Otieno, who stands 10 m away. Both somehow get the same height. Learners predict why the triangles formed can give the same answer. Groups then measure three printed right-angled triangles (A, B and C) that all have a 35° angle but different sizes, and record adjacent, opposite and hypotenuse in cm. Triangle A has sides 4.0, 2.8 and 4.9 cm; B has 8.0, 5.6 and 9.8 cm; C has 12.0, 8.4 and 14.7 cm. Learners calculate opposite/hypotenuse, adjacent/hypotenuse and opposite/adjacent for each triangle and find that every triangle gives about 0.571, 0.816 and 0.700 (real measurements vary by about ±0.02). In the Explain phase the teacher names the ratios sine, cosine and tangent (sin, cos, tan afterwards), and learners check on a calculator in DEG mode that sin 35° = 0.5736, cos 35° = 0.8192 and tan 35° = 0.7002. They connect the constant ratio to the tank: the ratio opposite ÷ adjacent depends only on the angle, not on the triangle size, which is why 8 m with 37° and 10 m with 31° can lead to one height. The DQB is updated and the class tank model is revised. Learners do not yet calculate the tank height; that is Lesson 4.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners look at the Lesson 1 diagram of the tank tower with Wanjiru (8 m) and Otieno (10 m) at different distances. Madam Achieng draws two right-angled triangles on the board, one small and one large, with the same angle at the bottom. In pairs learners individually write a prediction: 'If two right-angled triangles have the same angle but different sizes, what do you think stays the same and what changes?' They sketch the two triangles and mark opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse relative to the angle (building on Lesson 1). They share ideas with a partner and write their best prediction on a sticky note: 'I think ___ stays the same because ___.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Remember Wanjiru and Otieno at Kilimani Secondary School in Nakuru. Wanjiru is closer and gets a bigger angle. Yet both find the same tank height. Today we find out what stays the same.' Draw the two triangles with a 35° angle. Ask: 'Which sides get bigger when the triangle gets bigger? Which angle does not change?' Give 60 seconds of silent individual thinking, then pair talk for 2 minutes. WAIT TIME: after asking 'What do you think stays the same?', wait 10-15 seconds before taking answers. Cold-call 4 learners to share predictions, including at least 2 who have not spoken yet, and say: 'Thank you, I am not saying right or wrong yet. We will test it with evidence.' Record the predictions on the board under 'Our predictions'. Circulate and note any learner who says 'the ratio' unprompted.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction with a sketch (Developing and Using Models): learners commit to an idea before seeing data so they can later compare their reasoning with evidence. Writing the 'because' part makes their prior thinking visible and creates a reason to measure.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Learner sketches show correctly labelled opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse relative to the marked angle (Lesson 1 skill). (2) Learner states that the angle stays the same. (3) Tally the predictions: sides stay the same, a relationship between sides stays the same, or nothing stays the same. If more than a third mislabel the sides, spend 3 minutes re-labelling a triangle with the door frame before the Observe phase.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4, learners receive printed right-angled triangles A, B and C, all with a 35° angle and with the right angle at the bottom right. Each learner has a ruler and a pencil. They measure adjacent, opposite and hypotenuse for each triangle to the nearest 0.1 cm and record the lengths in a table. The expected ideal values are: A 4.0, 2.8, 4.9 cm; B 8.0, 5.6, 9.8 cm; C 12.0, 8.4, 14.7 cm. Next they use a calculator to work out opposite ÷ hypotenuse, adjacent ÷ hypotenuse and opposite ÷ adjacent for each triangle to 3 decimal places. Expected ratios: 0.571, 0.816 and 0.700 for every triangle, with real learner measurements varying by about ±0.02. Groups then compare the ratio columns across the three triangles and write what they notice in one sentence.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute materials, with 2 learners sharing a ruler. Say: 'Label the 35° angle first. Then name each side from that angle: opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse.' Model the first measurement for Triangle A on the board with 'The adjacent side is next to the 35° angle, and it is not the hypotenuse.' Assign roles: measurer, recorder, calculator operator, checker, rotating every triangle. Circulate with these questions: 'Which side is the longest? Does your hypotenuse look longest?' and 'Measure from the corner, not from the ruler's edge.' Check pairs: if a group gets ratios differing by more than 0.03, ask them to re-measure the side that seems off. After the ratio calculations say: 'Put your pencils down. Look at the three columns. What do you notice?' WAIT TIME: wait 10-15 seconds in silence. Then cold-call 3 groups to read out their Triangle A, B and C ratios for one column and record them on a class table on the board. Ask: 'Triangle C is three times as big as Triangle A. Did the ratio become three times as big?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data table pattern-finding (Analyzing and Interpreting Data): learners generate their own data and compare columns to find an invariant. The class pooled table shows that small measurement errors do not hide the pattern, which builds trust in the evidence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Lengths are measured to 0.1 cm and sides are labelled correctly from the 35° angle. (2) Ratios are computed correctly and in the expected range (about 0.57, 0.82, 0.70 within ±0.02). (3) Learners state that the ratios are about the same even though the triangles differ in size. Check each group's table with a quick tick and watch for learners dividing in the wrong order. Note any group still believing the ratio grows with the triangle, and revisit its table with it.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners explain in their groups why the ratios stayed the same: the three triangles are enlargements of one another with the same angles, so the sides are in proportion (linking to similarity from Strand 2.1). Madam Achieng then gives the names: the ratio opposite ÷ hypotenuse is called the sine of the angle (sin), adjacent ÷ hypotenuse is the cosine (cos), and opposite ÷ adjacent is the tangent (tan). Learners write the definitions in their notebooks: sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse, tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent. They set their calculators to DEG mode and check sin 35° = 0.5736, cos 35° = 0.8192 and tan 35° = 0.7002 against their class table, and discuss why the calculator values are slightly different from the hand-measured 0.571, 0.816 and 0.700 (measuring with a ruler to 0.1 cm has small errors). In pairs they then answer: 'How does this explain Wanjiru and Otieno getting the same tank height?' The expected idea is that tan of the angle gives the ratio of the height above eye level to the distance, and the angle tells us that ratio regardless of how far away the person stands. They do not yet calculate the height.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Why might the ratios stay the same? Think about similar shapes: if a triangle is enlarged, what happens to all its sides?' WAIT TIME: wait 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners. Introduce the names: 'Mathematicians gave these three ratios names. Opposite over hypotenuse is the sine. Adjacent over hypotenuse is the cosine. Opposite over adjacent is the tangent. We write sin, cos and tan.' Write the three definitions on the board. Say: 'Switch your calculator to DEG mode. Type sin 35 and read me the answer.' Check every pair's screen, because RAD mode is a common error. Ask: 'Our hand answer was 0.571 and the calculator says 0.5736. Why are they close but not identical?' Cold-call 2 learners. Then link to the phenomenon: 'Wanjiru reads 37° and Otieno reads 31°. The tangent changes with the angle, but for any one angle it does not change with the size of the triangle. How could that help them both find the same height?' Give 2 minutes of pair talk and cold-call 3 pairs. Confirm: 'Next lesson we use these to find sides, and Lesson 4 gives the full tank calculation.' Do not use SOH-CAH-TOA yet beyond a brief mention if learners ask.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (Constructing Explanations): learners state the claim (the ratios depend only on the angle), cite their table as evidence, and reason with similarity (enlargement keeps the sides in proportion). Naming the ratios after the discovery gives the vocabulary meaning.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Learners write sin, cos and tan definitions correctly in terms of opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse. (2) Calculator in DEG mode gives 0.5736, 0.8192 and 0.7002 for 35°. (3) Learners explain that the ratio stays the same because the triangles are similar or in proportion. (4) Learners link the idea to the tank in a sentence such as 'The angle fixes the ratio, so the distance does not change the answer.' Use a 3-question exit check: write the formula for tan θ; state sin 35° to 4 decimal places; state what stays the same when a triangle is enlarged. Common errors to look for: inverted ratios and RAD mode.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the Driving Question Board with the driving question: 'How can we use the angles and one side of a right-angled triangle to find any unknown height or distance in our environment, without ever measuring it directly?' The board has three columns: 'Questions', 'Answered' and 'New understandings'. Groups review the Lesson 1 sticky notes and move any question now answered, such as 'Why do different angles give the same height?' (partly answered), to 'Answered' or add a note. Each group writes at least one 'New understanding' on a sticky note, e.g. 'For 35°, opposite ÷ adjacent is always about 0.70' or 'Ratios stay the same for any size of triangle at the same angle.' They also add one new question, e.g. 'How do we use tan to find the height of the tank?' or 'Why do sin and cos use the hypotenuse?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Walk to the board with your group. Read the questions from Lesson 1. Which can we now answer, even partly?' Allow 3 minutes. Ask a group to read a note aloud and ask: 'What evidence from today's table supports moving it?' Press for evidence rather than opinions. WAIT TIME: wait 10-15 seconds after asking 'What new question do we have?' and cold-call 3 groups to read their new question. Sort the new questions by theme: using the ratios to find a side, the angle of elevation, building a clinometer. Say: 'Keep your question; we will answer it in the coming lessons.' Make sure that quieter learners also post notes by asking each group to name a different writer than last time.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Public question tracking (Asking Questions and Defining Problems): the DQB makes the growth in understanding visible. Moving notes between columns requires learners to cite evidence, and new questions point to the next lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Each group moves or annotates at least one note with a piece of evidence from the triangle table. (2) New understanding notes state the constant-ratio idea in the learner's own words. (3) New questions are specific and testable (e.g. about using tan to find height). Look for groups still posting only vague questions and prompt them with 'Which triangle side would you know and which would you want?'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise the class tank model begun in Lesson 1. On a large chart, the class redraws the tank tower diagram with Wanjiru at 8 m and Otieno at 10 m, showing two right-angled triangles with different angles but both reaching the same height. Beside the diagram, learners add a 'Ratio box' with the definitions of sin, cos and tan and the calculator values for 35°. They add a sentence in their own notebooks: 'The ratio opposite ÷ adjacent depends only on the angle, not on the size of the triangle, so it can be used to find a height from a distance.' Each learner then updates their personal model by adding one thing that changed since the Predict phase, and writes a one-line answer to: 'What do I still need to know to find the tank height?' Expected answers: how to use the ratio with a known side, and how to measure the angle.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the Lesson 1 chart and say: 'Our model last time had the tank, the two learners and the side names. What do we add today?' Draw the diagram with student input, and ask: 'Where is the angle? Which side is opposite? Which is adjacent?' Add the ratio box as learners dictate it. Ask for an updated explanation: 'Why do both learners get the same height?' WAIT TIME: wait 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners to give a part of the explanation, each adding to the previous. Be careful not to compute the height; say: 'We do not yet calculate. That is Lesson 4, when we choose the right ratio and solve.' Hand out the summary table (Observed, Learned, Explained) and have learners complete it individually in 4 minutes. Collect it or check it at the door. Close with: 'Next time we explore a pattern between sine and cosine for different angles.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision (Developing and Using Models): learners add the new idea of a constant ratio to the shared tank model, linking the explanation to the phenomenon and showing what remains unexplained. The 'What I still need to know' step keeps the driving question open.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) The revised diagram shows both triangles with opposite and adjacent sides labelled and the angle marked. (2) Learners' sentences state that the ratio depends on the angle and not on triangle size. (3) Learners avoid claiming that the angle itself changes with triangle size. (4) The 'still need to know' note identifies using the ratio to find an unknown side or measuring the angle. Check the Observed/Learned/Explained summary tables to decide who needs a short reteach of the three ratios in the next lesson.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: (1) Did learners discover the constant ratio from their own measurements, or did they rely on my statement? Which groups needed prompting? (2) Which sides did learners mislabel, and did this come from confusion between adjacent and hypotenuse? (3) How many learners had their calculator in RAD mode, and what routine will I use to check DEG mode in future lessons? (4) Did the small differences between hand-measured ratios (about 0.571, 0.816, 0.700) and calculator values (0.5736, 0.8192, 0.7002) support or confuse the idea of a constant ratio? (5) Could learners connect the constant ratio to Wanjiru and Otieno getting the same height? (6) Which learners have not yet spoken in a whole-class discussion, and how will I include them next time? (7) What should be adjusted for Lesson 3 on complementary angles?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: What did you measure and calculate for the three 35° triangles A, B and C? Record the adjacent, opposite and hypotenuse lengths, and the three ratios (opposite ÷ hypotenuse, adjacent ÷ hypotenuse, opposite ÷ adjacent) for each triangle. What did you notice about the ratios as the triangles got bigger?
summaryTablePrompt.learned: What are sin θ, cos θ and tan θ in terms of opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse? What are the calculator values of sin 35°, cos 35° and tan 35° in DEG mode, and how close are they to your measured ratios?
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Why do the ratios stay the same for triangles of different sizes with the same angle? How does this idea help explain how Wanjiru (8 m, 37°) and Otieno (10 m, 31°) at Kilimani Secondary School can both find the same tank height without climbing the tower? What do you still need to learn to calculate that height?

LESSONS.title: Complementary Angles: Why Does sin 20° Equal cos 70°?
LESSONS.aresKeywords: complementary angles, sine, cosine, opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse, right-angled triangle, calculator DEG mode, Kilimani water tank

slo.purpose: To discover and explain why the sine of an acute angle equals the cosine of its complement, so that learners can choose between sin and cos with confidence when they use the ratios to find the height of the Kilimani Secondary School water tank.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (c) relate sines and cosines of complementary angles. Learners will state that sin θ = cos(90° - θ) and cos θ = sin(90° - θ), and explain that the side opposite one acute angle is the side adjacent to the other acute angle.
slo.skills: Using the Lesson 2 definitions of sin and cos to calculate ratios in a right-angled triangle; using a calculator in DEG mode to generate a table of complementary angles; identifying patterns in data (SEP: Analyzing and Interpreting Data); constructing an explanation from a labelled diagram (SEP: Constructing Explanations); making generalisations and conclusions from a table.
slo.attitudes: Self-efficacy: the learner makes observations and establishes the relationships between the sine and cosine ratios. Learning to learn: the learner learns collaboratively with peers. Love: the learner shows care for others by listening and sharing the calculator in turn.
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 2 gave learners the definitions of sin, cos and tan and showed that the ratios depend only on the angle. Lesson 3 asks: when the angle is the other acute angle of the triangle, how do the ratios change? The answer, that sin and cos swap, means learners need fewer tools, and it checks the later use of the tank triangle from either acute angle. Lesson 4 will use the ratios to solve for unknown sides, including the tank-height calculation for Wanjiru (8 m, 37°) and Otieno (10 m, 31°).
slo.safetyNotes: Keep the calculator on the desk and share it in turn. Use rulers and set squares carefully and do not point them at others. Keep bags and walkways clear while learners move to the board to add entries.

LESSONS.overview: Madam Achieng reminds the class of the puzzle at Kilimani Secondary School, Nakuru: Wanjiru (8 m away) and Otieno (10 m away) sight the top of the tank tower and read different angles, yet the tank height must come out the same. In Lesson 2 learners found that sin, cos and tan depend on the angle, not on the size of the triangle. Today they notice that every right-angled triangle has two acute angles, and ask what happens to the ratios if we look from the OTHER acute angle. Learners first predict, then fill in a table of complementary pairs (20° and 70°, 30° and 60°, 35° and 55°, 45° and 45°) using a calculator in DEG mode, and then draw and label one triangle twice to explain why sin θ = cos(90° - θ). They add questions and answers to the Driving Question Board and revise the class model of how the tank height can be found from an angle and a distance.

framework.learnerExperience: (Approx. 12 minutes) Learners look at the Lesson 1 sketch of the tank tower on the wall. In pairs they draw a right-angled triangle for Wanjiru (the tower is the vertical side, the ground is the horizontal side, her line of sight is the hypotenuse). They mark her angle of elevation at her eye and then mark the OTHER acute angle at the top. They write: (1) How big is the other acute angle if one is 37°? (2) If Wanjiru's angle is 37°, what do you predict sin and cos of the OTHER angle will be compared with sin 37° and cos 37°? They write the prediction in their books with a reason, using a sentence starter: 'I think the sin of the other angle will be ___ because ___.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Remember Wanjiru at Kilimani Secondary School. Every right-angled triangle has TWO acute angles. We have only looked at one. Today we look at the other.' Draw the triangle with the 90° corner and ask: 'If the three angles add to 180° and one is 90°, what do the two acute angles add up to?' WAIT TIME 10 seconds, then cold-call 2 learners. Introduce the word complementary: two angles that add to 90°. Give 3 minutes of silent individual thinking, then 3 minutes of pair talk. Say: 'I am not looking for the right answer yet. I want your best guess and your reason.' Cold-call 4 pairs with the sentence starter and record 4 predictions on the board without judging them. Do not confirm or correct.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Share-Revise (Think-Pair-Share): writing a prediction with a reason before any data are seen exposes learners' current ideas (for example 'the ratios will stay the same' or 'they will be opposite') so that the later table can confirm or challenge each idea. This keeps the phenomenon of the tank triangle in view.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) learners who correctly state the other acute angle as 90° minus the first (53° for 37°); (2) learners who write a reason rather than just a guess; (3) learners who mark the top angle at the correct vertex. Walk round and tick on a class list who gave a reason. If more than a third give 53° wrongly, redraw the angle sum on the board before moving on.

framework.learnerExperience: (Approx. 25 minutes) In groups of 4 with one calculator set to DEG mode per pair, learners complete the Lesson 3 table. For each pair of complementary angles they find the sin and cos to 4 decimal places: 20° and 70° (sin 20° = 0.3420, cos 20° = 0.9397, sin 70° = 0.9397, cos 70° = 0.3420); 30° and 60° (sin 30° = 0.5000, cos 30° = 0.8660, sin 60° = 0.8660, cos 60° = 0.5000); 35° and 55° (sin 35° = 0.5736, cos 35° = 0.8192, sin 55° = 0.8192, cos 55° = 0.5736); 45° and 45° (sin 45° = cos 45° = 0.7071). Rows are shared among group members and the results are pooled. Learners then circle values that match and write what they notice. They check that the 35° row agrees with the calculator value they used in Lesson 2 (sin 35° = 0.5736, cos 35° = 0.8192). Extension: they predict sin 80° from the table of cos 10° and test it.
framework.teacherMoves: Before starting, say: 'Check the top of your calculator screen for D or DEG. If it shows R or G, change it now. That is the commonest mistake.' Walk round and check 3 calculators in each row of desks. Say: 'Fill the table, then circle numbers that are equal. Do not explain yet.' Ask: 'What do you notice when you look across the row for 20° and 70°?' WAIT TIME 10 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners to read out what they circled. Ask: 'Is it a coincidence for 20° and 70°? What about 30° and 60°?' Cold-call 2 more groups to report their other rows. For groups finishing early, ask: 'Why do you think 45° gives the same value for sin and cos?' Do not give the reason yet. Collect findings on the class chart: 'sin of one angle = cos of the other'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Pattern Finding in Data (Analyzing and Interpreting Data): learners generate a table from the calculator, look for repeated values across rows and compare predictions with data. Using four different angle pairs shows that the pattern is not a coincidence, and the 45° case acts as a special check.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) calculators in DEG mode with correct values to 4 d.p.; (2) learners circling sin 20° with cos 70° (and not sin 20° with sin 70°); (3) learners checking that the two angles in each row add to 90°; (4) a statement such as 'the sine of one angle equals the cosine of the other'. Record on a tally sheet which groups noticed the pattern unprompted. Listen for groups who say '45° is the same both ways' and invite them to share later.

framework.learnerExperience: (Approx. 25 minutes) Learners explain WHY the pattern occurs. Each learner draws a right-angled triangle with a 35° angle at A and 55° at B, with sides labelled a (opposite A), b (opposite B) and c (hypotenuse). They complete two tables: relative to angle A (35°) the opposite side is a and the adjacent side is b; relative to angle B (55°) the opposite side is b and the adjacent side is a. They write sin 35° = a/c and cos 55° = a/c, then cos 35° = b/c and sin 55° = b/c. They state the rule in their own words, then write it with symbols: sin θ = cos(90° - θ) and cos θ = sin(90° - θ). They test it with Wanjiru's tank triangle: her angle is 37°, so the angle at the top of the sight line is 53°, which gives sin 37° = cos 53° and cos 37° = sin 53°. They use the rule to answer: if sin 25° is known, what is cos 65°? Why is sin 45° = cos 45°? Finally they revisit their predictions and mark them 'supported' or 'revise'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Your table shows WHAT happens. Now we explain WHY. Use your triangle labels.' Model the first label on the board, then let learners do the second. Ask: 'The side opposite 35° is the side a. Which side is next to 55° but not the hypotenuse?' WAIT TIME 10 seconds, cold-call 3 learners. Ask: 'So what happens to the opposite and adjacent sides when we change from the 35° angle to the 55° angle?' WAIT TIME 15 seconds, cold-call 2 learners to say it in a full sentence: 'The opposite side becomes the adjacent side.' Then ask: 'Why does 45° give equal sin and cos?' Guide: the two acute angles are both 45°, so the opposite and adjacent sides are the same length. Press for reasoning with 'How do you know?' and 'Show me on the diagram.' Address a common error: some learners write sin 20° = cos 20°. Ask them to check on the calculator. Invite learners to compare their prediction from the start and say whether it was supported. Remind them not to use the ratios to find sides yet; that is Lesson 4.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (Constructing Explanations): the claim is 'sin θ = cos(90° - θ)', the evidence is the table from the calculator, and the reasoning is the swap of opposite and adjacent sides in the labelled triangle. Linking the number pattern to the diagram builds a causal explanation, not just a rule to memorise.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) a triangle with the opposite and adjacent sides correctly relabelled for each angle; (2) a full-sentence reason that uses the words opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse; (3) the rule written correctly with 90° - θ; (4) a correct answer for cos 65° (equals sin 25°) and for the 45° case. Use a quick exit check: 'Write cos 40° as a sine.' Expected answer: sin 50°. Note learners who answer sin 40° for follow-up in the next lesson.

framework.learnerExperience: (Approx. 8 minutes) Learners go to the Driving Question Board, which has three columns: Questions, Answered and New understandings. They write on sticky notes any new questions the lesson raised (for example 'Can we use the 53° angle at the top of the tank instead of 37°?' or 'Does the same swap work for tan?' or 'How do we find the actual height using these ratios?'). They move any questions that are now answered from Questions to Answered (for example 'Do sin and cos always depend on the angle only?' from Lesson 2) and add a note in New understandings: 'sin of an angle = cos of its complement because opposite and adjacent swap.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Come to the DQB in your groups. Each group adds at least one question and one new understanding.' Ask: 'Which question is Lesson 3 helping us to answer? Which is still waiting?' WAIT TIME 10 seconds. Cold-call 3 groups to read a sticky note aloud. Help the class to see that 'How tall is the tank?' is still in the Questions column and that the next lesson will use the ratios to find unknown sides. Praise questions that use the vocabulary opposite, adjacent and complementary. If no one asks about tan, prompt: 'We have only looked at sin and cos. What about tan?' and add it as a class question without answering it.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Question Tracking on the DQB: moving questions to Answered and writing New understandings makes the growth of knowledge visible and keeps the class focused on the tank phenomenon. It also uses learners' own questions to set the direction for the next lesson.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) questions that connect to the tank (heights, other angle, using sin or cos to find lengths); (2) correct wording in New understandings, using complementary and opposite/adjacent; (3) at least one question from each group. Note any recurring misconception, such as 'sin and cos are the same', to address at the start of Lesson 4.

framework.learnerExperience: (Approx. 10 minutes) Learners open the class model of the tank problem started in Lesson 1 and updated in Lesson 2. In pairs they add a new part: on the tank diagram (a vertical tower of unknown height, Wanjiru standing 8 m away with a 37° angle of elevation) they mark the second acute angle at the top of the sight line as 53° and write beside it 'sin 37° = cos 53°, cos 37° = sin 53°'. Under the diagram they write a new rule for the model: 'Either acute angle can be used. Sin and cos swap when we move to the complementary angle.' They do the same quickly for Otieno (10 m, 31°) and mark his complement as 59°. They write a new sentence about what they still need: 'We know the ratios depend only on the angle, and that sin and cos are linked. We still need a way to use a ratio to find the tank height.' Then they complete the exit ticket: 'Write cos 70° as a sine and explain in one sentence why it works.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open the model. What has changed since yesterday? Mark in a different colour pen what we added today.' Ask: 'Look at Otieno's triangle. What is his other acute angle? How do you know?' WAIT TIME 10 seconds, cold-call 3 learners. Prompt: 'Does this solve the height? What is still missing?' Cold-call 2 learners to say what they still need. Make the link: 'Next lesson you will choose the correct ratio from the side you know and the side you want, and solve for the unknown side. That is how Wanjiru and Otieno will find the same tank height.' Collect the exit tickets at the door. Do not reveal the height of the tank.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision (Developing and Using Models): learners add the complementary-angle relationship to a diagram they have already built, so that the model of the tank grows lesson by lesson. Identifying what is still missing prepares them for the use of ratios to find unknown sides in Lesson 4.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) both acute angles marked correctly on each learner's triangle (53° and 59°); (2) the correct rule written; (3) an explicit statement of what is still needed (a way to find the unknown side). On the exit ticket, check that cos 70° is written as sin 20° with a reason that mentions opposite and adjacent swapping. Sort the tickets into correct, partly correct (right answer, no reason) and incorrect to plan the first five minutes of Lesson 4.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson ask yourself: (1) Did learners explain the pattern using the swap of opposite and adjacent sides, or did they only copy the rule sin θ = cos(90° - θ)? (2) Which learners confused sin 20° = cos 70° with sin 20° = sin 70°, and what diagram will help them? (3) Were all calculators in DEG mode, and did any learners need support with the buttons? (4) Did the wait time give quieter learners, including girls and learners who speak mostly Kiswahili or mother tongue, space to share? (5) How well did learners connect the lesson to Wanjiru and Otieno at Kilimani Secondary School? Note which exit tickets need follow-up before Lesson 4, where learners choose a ratio and solve for an unknown side. Do not reveal the tank height, since the class will work towards it in Lessons 4 to 8.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Complete the Lesson 3 table. For the pairs 20°/70°, 30°/60°, 35°/55° and 45°/45°, we found that sin of one angle equals cos of the other (for example sin 20° = cos 70° = 0.3420 and sin 35° = cos 55° = 0.5736). At 45° the sine and cosine are equal (0.7071).
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Two acute angles in a right-angled triangle add up to 90° and are called complementary. The side opposite one angle is the side adjacent to the other. So sin θ = cos(90° - θ) and cos θ = sin(90° - θ). Wanjiru's 37° at the tank goes with 53° at the top of her line of sight.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Write in your own words why sin 35° = cos 55°, using the words opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse, and say how this helps us get closer to finding the height of the Kilimani Secondary School water tank without climbing it.
