LESSONS.title: Choosing the Right Ratio: Solving for Unknown Sides and the First Full Tank-Height Calculation
LESSONS.aresKeywords: sine, cosine, tangent, opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse, unknown side, equation, angle of elevation, eye height, Kilimani Secondary School, Nakuru

slo.purpose: Learners choose the correct trigonometric ratio from the known side and the wanted side, set up an equation and solve for an unknown side. They use this to complete the first full tank-height calculation from Wanjiru's data (8 m, 37°).
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: determine the sine, cosine and tangent of acute angles in a right-angled triangle and use them to find unknown sides; identify the right-angled triangle in relation to a particular angle (hypotenuse, opposite, adjacent); apply trigonometric ratios to find unknown heights and distances; recognise the use of trigonometry in real-life situations.
slo.skills: Labelling a triangle from the angle theta; matching known and wanted sides to sin, cos or tan; rearranging an equation to solve for an unknown side; using a scientific calculator in DEG mode; giving trig values to 4 d.p. and final lengths to 1 d.p. with units. NGSS-aligned practices: Developing and Using Models (labelled diagrams), Analyzing and Interpreting Data, Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking, Constructing Explanations.
slo.attitudes: Core competencies: Self-efficacy (the learner builds confidence by solving real problems with ratios); Learning to learn (the learner learns collaboratively in pairs). Value: Love (the learner shows a caring attitude to others by helping peers check their working). PCI: Self-esteem (the learner gains self-esteem in solving problems that look impossible at first).
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1 and 2 gave learners the side names and the constant ratios sin, cos and tan. Lesson 4 turns those ratios into a problem-solving tool. Learners use them to calculate Wanjiru's height for the tank for the first time (8 m, 37°, giving 7.5 m). This is the first answer to the driving question and sets up the clinometer in Lesson 5. Lesson 3 is used only as a check that sin and cos are interchangeable between complementary angles. Inverse ratios (finding an angle) are not taught; all angles are given.
slo.safetyNotes: Learners do no outdoor work in this lesson. Remind them to keep rulers and compasses away from faces and to pack away drawing tools after use. Check that calculators are in DEG mode before starting. Do not let anyone climb the water tank tower or the frame, even when the tank is discussed.

LESSONS.overview: Madam Achieng reopens the tank problem: Wanjiru stands 8 m from the tower at Kilimani Secondary School, Nakuru, and reads 37°. Learners predict how they could use the constant ratios from Lesson 2 to turn that into a height. They then work through a 3-step method: (1) label the triangle from the angle theta, (2) pick the ratio that links the KNOWN side and the WANTED side, (3) write the equation, solve and state the answer with units. They practise on Kisumu roof rafter, Kericho stream and Mombasa mango tree problems, and a check on a Kisumu rafter shows sin and cos giving the same answer through complementary angles. Finally they use the same method on Wanjiru's data, adding the 1.5 m eye height to get 7.5 m. The Driving Question Board is updated and the class model gains a 'choose the ratio, solve for the side' step.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners see a sketch of the tank tower with Wanjiru 8 m from the base and the angle 37° marked. They are told that the height of the top of the tank above her eye level is the unknown, x. In pairs they write: (1) which side of the triangle they know, which they want, and which ratio might link them, and (2) a rough guess of x with a reason, remembering that the 35° triangles in Lesson 2 all had tan = 0.700 whatever their size. They record predictions on mini-whiteboards or in their books and hold them up.
framework.teacherMoves: Draw the right-angled triangle on the board: Wanjiru at one corner, the tower base at the right angle, the tank top at the third corner. Say: 'Wanjiru knows 8 m and 37°. She never climbed the tower. Which ratio could help her, and why?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds in silence. Then cold-call 4 learners, including at least 2 who did not volunteer, and ask each: 'Which side is known, which side is wanted?' Do not confirm or correct. Write all ideas on the board under 'Our predictions'. Say: 'Keep your prediction. We will test it today.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction and Reasoning from Prior Evidence: learners use Lesson 2's discovery that ratios stay constant to make a testable claim BEFORE any new method is taught. This exposes the idea that the ratio is what links a known side to a wanted side, and gives the class something to confirm or revise later.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check whether learners (a) label 8 m as adjacent and the tank height as opposite relative to 37°, (b) name tan or at least give opposite and adjacent as the sides involved, (c) give a reason that uses the idea of constant ratios. Tally on a clipboard how many pairs name tan. Learners who confuse opposite and adjacent are flagged for support during the Observe Phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in pairs through a guided 3-step worked example, then carry out 3 practice tasks with a calculator in DEG mode. Step 1: label the triangle from theta (hypotenuse, opposite, adjacent). Step 2: write down the KNOWN side and the WANTED side and pick the ratio that has both (tan for opposite and adjacent, sin for opposite and hypotenuse, cos for adjacent and hypotenuse). Step 3: write the equation, rearrange and solve. Tasks: (a) Kisumu roof rafter: horizontal span 3.6 m, rafter makes 30° with the horizontal, so rafter = 3.6 / cos 30 = 3.6 / 0.8660 = 4.2 m (4.16 m). (b) Kericho stream: a learner on the bank opposite a tree walks 20 m along the bank, the line of sight to the tree makes 40° with the bank, so width = 20 x tan 40 = 20 x 0.8391 = 16.8 m. (c) Mombasa mango tree: 12 m from the base, elevation 28°, eye height 1.5 m, so height = 12 x tan 28 + 1.5 = 12 x 0.5317 + 1.5 = 6.38 + 1.5 = 7.9 m. They record each task in a 4-column table: known side, wanted side, ratio chosen, answer.
framework.teacherMoves: Model Task (a) on the board with a think-aloud: 'The span 3.6 m is next to the 30° angle, so it is ADJACENT. The rafter is opposite the right angle, so it is the HYPOTENUSE. Adjacent and hypotenuse, which ratio is that?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners for the ratio and the reason. Show how to rearrange cos 30 = 3.6 / rafter into rafter = 3.6 / cos 30 and point out that the unknown is on the bottom. Then release pairs to do (b) and (c) alone. Circulate with the prompt: 'Show me which side is known and which is wanted before you touch the calculator.' Check DEG mode on at least 5 calculators. For fast pairs ask: 'Mombasa mango tree: what does the 1.5 m add, and why?' As a check, ask pairs to use the complementary angle 60° with sin 60 = 0.8660 for (a) and compare; this is only a check, since complementary angles were taught in Lesson 3.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured Problem-Solving Routine (Known-Wanted-Ratio table): the 4-column table makes the decision step visible. Learners see that the ratio is chosen by which two sides are involved, not by guessing. Comparing answers across three different contexts shows that the same reasoning works for rafters, rivers and trees. This links directly to the tank problem.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (a) correct labelling of the sides before calculation, (b) correct ratio chosen in all 3 tasks, (c) the equation written before the calculator is used, (d) answers within 0.1 of 4.2 m, 16.8 m and 7.9 m, (e) eye height of 1.5 m added in task (c). Note common errors (using sin for adjacent and opposite, multiplying when you should divide, calculator in RAD mode, forgetting the 1.5 m) and tally them on the board for the Explain Phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the anchoring phenomenon and solve it themselves, step by step, using Wanjiru's data (8 m from the tower, 37°, eye height 1.5 m). In pairs they: (1) draw and label the triangle (right angle at the tower base level with her eye, theta = 37°, adjacent = 8 m, opposite = unknown); (2) name the ratio: opposite and adjacent, so tan; (3) write tan 37 = x / 8, so x = 8 x tan 37 = 8 x 0.7536 = 6.03 m above eye level; (4) add the eye height: 6.03 + 1.5 = 7.53 m, which rounds to 7.5 m. Then they compare their solution with the other tasks and write 2-3 sentences: 'We choose the ratio by ... The tank is 7.5 m high because ...'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Remember this sketch? This morning you predicted. Now you will test it.' Do NOT tell the answer. Give 4 minutes for pairs to work. Circulate and ask: 'Why 8 x tan 37 and not 8 / tan 37?' Hold a whole-class discussion. Cold-call 3 pairs, choosing pairs with different working, e.g. one that forgot the 1.5 m and one that added it. Ask: 'Why does the answer 6.03 m not give the height from the ground?' WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before each call. Ask: 'Compare with your prediction: what did you get right, and what do you want to change?' Then raise the key idea: 'The ratio tan 37 = 0.7536 depends only on the angle, so Wanjiru can use it at any distance.' Preview, without solving, that Otieno stands 10 m away at 31°, so the class can see in Lesson 8 whether his answer matches.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with Prediction Revisit: learners state a claim (the height is 7.5 m), support it with evidence (the calculation) and give reasoning (the ratio depends only on the angle, so it links the 8 m to the height). Revisiting their own predictions turns the lesson into a conceptual change, not only a procedure.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect each pair's written solution. Success criteria: labelled diagram, tan chosen with a reason, correct equation, 6.03 m (accept 6.0 m), eye height added, final answer 7.5 m with units, and a sentence linking to constant ratios. Use a 3-point check: all 6 steps (secure), 4-5 steps (developing), fewer than 4 (needs support). Plan a small support group for the next lesson.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit the class DQB with its three columns, 'Questions', 'Answered' and 'New understandings'. On sticky notes in pairs they (1) move at least one question to 'Answered', for example 'Which ratio do we use to find the height from the distance and the angle?' with the answer 'tan, because the 8 m is adjacent and the height is opposite'; (2) add 'New understandings', for example 'We pick the ratio by the known and the wanted side' and 'We must add 1.5 m eye height'; and (3) add a new question, for example 'How do we measure the angle in the first place without a protractor on the tower?' or 'Does Otieno get the same height from 10 m and 31 degrees?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at the board. Which question can we now answer, and what is your evidence?' WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners to place a sticky note and justify it. Insist on evidence: 'Which calculation shows that?' Praise good new questions such as the clinometer one and say: 'That is exactly where we are going next lesson.' Do not answer the Otieno question; say: 'We will test that with real data.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a Public Record of Learning: learners see their own questions get answered and new ones appear. This keeps the whole sequence coherent, shows how each lesson moves the work toward the final clinometer measurement, and builds ownership of the investigation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that notes moved to 'Answered' cite a calculation or a diagram as evidence, that the 'New understandings' column includes the idea of choosing the ratio from the known and wanted sides, and that at least 5 new questions are linked to measuring angles or to Otieno's data. Note learners who add no questions.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise their class model of the tank problem. In pairs they redraw their model diagram: the tower, Wanjiru at 8 m, the 37° angle, the labelled sides (adjacent 8 m, opposite unknown, hypotenuse the line of sight), and add a new 'Choose and solve' box with 3 steps: label the sides, pick the ratio from the known and wanted side, write the equation and solve. They add a note in a different colour: 'Height above ground = distance x tan(angle) + 1.5 m'. They then add a line, 'Why it works: the ratio depends only on the angle, not on the size of the triangle'. Finally they add a short flowchart: Known side + wanted side leads to sin, cos or tan.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Your model must now show how a number is produced, not only what the sides are called.' Give 6 minutes. Circulate and ask: 'Where does your model show why 8 m and 37 degrees are enough?' Cold-call 3 pairs to show models and ask the class: 'Does this model explain Wanjiru's answer? What is still missing?' WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. Draw out the gap: 'How do we actually get 37 degrees from the tower?' Leave the class with the gap for Lesson 5. Optional extension for early finishers: use a complementary angle to check the tank answer using sin and cos, as a Lesson 3 check only.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision: learners add the new 'choose and solve' mechanism to their earlier models, building the explanation of the phenomenon in layers. Marking the changes in a different colour shows how their understanding has grown since Lesson 1 and highlights the missing piece (measuring the angle), which motivates building the clinometer.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for models that (a) show correct labelling relative to 37°, (b) include the 3-step choose-and-solve process, (c) include the 1.5 m eye height in the formula, (d) state that the ratio depends on the angle only, and (e) identify a gap about measuring the angle. Use an exit ticket: 'A Kericho tree is 25 m away, elevation 30 degrees. Which ratio would you use to find the height above your eye, and why?' Collect and sort into secure, developing and needs support.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, review the paired solutions and exit tickets. Which ratio-choice errors were most common (sin vs tan, multiplying vs dividing)? Did learners explain WHY they chose the ratio, or just follow the steps? Did every learner remember to add the 1.5 m eye height? How many learners were secure on the tank calculation, and which learners need extra support before the clinometer in Lesson 5? Was WAIT TIME kept to 10-15 seconds, and did cold-calling include quieter learners? Which new DQB questions will guide Lesson 5, and were calculators in DEG mode throughout?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that to find an unknown side, we label the triangle from the angle, pick the ratio that links the KNOWN side and the WANTED side, write the equation and solve. In the tank problem, Wanjiru is 8 m away at 37 degrees, so 8 x tan 37 = 6.03 m above eye level, and with her 1.5 m eye height the top of the tank is 7.5 m.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that tan links opposite and adjacent, sin links opposite and hypotenuse, and cos links adjacent and hypotenuse. We learned that the ratio depends only on the angle, so one angle and one side are enough to find another side. We also learned to use tan 37 = 0.7536 in DEG mode and to add the 1.5 m eye height.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We can now partly explain how the tank height can be found without climbing it: the known distance and the angle give a ratio that lets us calculate the height. We still need to explain how to measure the angle accurately, and to check that Otieno (10 m, 31 degrees) gets the same height, which we will test in later lessons.

LESSONS.title: Angle of Elevation and Building the Clinometer
LESSONS.aresKeywords: angle of elevation, clinometer, protractor, string, washer, straw, horizontal, line of sight, complementary angles, tan, eye height 1.5 m, Kilimani Secondary School

slo.purpose: Learners define the angle of elevation, build a simple clinometer from a cardboard protractor, straw, string and washer, and read it correctly (angle = degrees between the string and the 90° mark). They test it on the classroom door frame and set up tan for the height, so the water-tank problem moves from calculation on paper to real measurement.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (1) define the angle of elevation as the angle above the horizontal from the observer's eye up to the object; (2) explain why the protractor reading is 90° minus the angle of elevation, using complementary angles; (3) read a clinometer, where the angle of elevation is the number of degrees between the string and the 90° mark when the straw is sighted on the object; (4) set up height = (distance × tan angle) + 1.5 m for a clinometer measurement.
slo.skills: Making a simple clinometer using locally available materials; measuring angles of elevation of objects in the immediate environment; reading a scale accurately to the nearest degree; modelling a real situation with a right-angled triangle; setting up tan for a height. NGSS-aligned practices: Developing and Using Models, Planning and Carrying Out Investigations, Constructing Explanations, Engaging in Argument from Evidence.
slo.attitudes: Love: the learner demonstrates a caring attitude to others when using the clinometer to measure the angle of elevation of objects in the immediate environment (taking turns, steadying a partner's reading). Learners also build self-efficacy and self-esteem by making and using their own instrument, and show responsibility in caring for the materials.
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1 to 4 gave learners the right-angled triangle model, the side names, the ratios sin, cos and tan, the complementary-angle link, and a method for solving for an unknown side. Lesson 5 turns the picture of Wanjiru's angle into a real instrument: learners learn what 'angle of elevation' means and build the clinometer they will use outdoors in Lesson 6 and to confirm the tank height in Lesson 8. Today they test it indoors on a target with a known height, the classroom door frame.
slo.safetyNotes: Use sharp scissors and pointed tools carefully. Pass scissors handle-first. Do not sight directly at the sun or bright windows through the straw. Keep the straw away from partners' eyes, and hold it against your own cheek. Washers swing, so do not swing them at classmates. Walk, do not run, while measuring distances in the classroom and keep bags out of the way. Measurements are taken on level ground or a level floor.

LESSONS.overview: Madam Achieng reopens the anchoring phenomenon: Wanjiru at Kilimani Secondary School in Nakuru stands 8 m from the tank tower and reads an angle of 37°. But how did she get that angle without climbing? Learners predict how a protractor, a string and a straw could capture an angle of looking upwards, then build a clinometer from a cardboard protractor, a straw taped along the straight edge, and a string with a washer hung from the centre mark. They observe that when the straw is horizontal the string hangs at the 90° mark, and when the straw is tilted up to sight an object the string moves away from 90°. The angle of elevation is the number of degrees between the string and the 90° mark. Learners connect this to complementary angles (the scale reading is 90° minus the angle of elevation). Finally they test the clinometer on the top of the classroom door frame, 2.1 m high, sighted from 3.0 m away with eye height 1.5 m. The expected angle is about 11°. Learners set up height = (3.0 × tan angle) + 1.5 m and compare with the known 2.1 m. They then add to the Driving Question Board and revise their cumulative model of how the tank height can be found without climbing.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners look at the Lesson 1 diagram of the tank tower with Wanjiru and Otieno. Madam Achieng shows a bare cardboard protractor, a straw, a piece of string and a washer. Individually in their notebooks (3 minutes) they answer: 'Wanjiru read 37° at the tank tower. How could these four items measure the angle at which she looks UP at the top of the tank? Draw your idea and label where the angle is.' They draw a sketch, then pair-share, then a few learners share with the class. Learners also predict: 'What do you think the string will do when the straw points straight ahead, and when it points up at the top of the tank?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Wanjiru never climbed the tank at Kilimani, yet she has an angle of 37°. Today we make the tool that gives us that angle.' Hold up the four items and say: 'Look at these items. Do not touch them yet.' Give 3 minutes of silent drawing, with WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after asking 'Where is the angle in your sketch?' before taking any answer. Circulate and note which learners draw the angle from the eye going up (the correct idea), from the ground, or at the top of the tank. Then say: 'Turn to your partner and explain your sketch in 1 minute.' Cold-call 3 pairs with different ideas and write the ideas on the board without judging. Ask: 'Why do you think the string will hang straight down whatever we do?' Take 2 responses. Record the predictions on chart paper to revisit in the Explain phase.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain with Sketch-and-Share: committing to a drawn prediction makes learners' existing ideas about angle and gravity visible. Later, comparing the sketch with the observed clinometer makes the conceptual change clear and gives learners ownership of the revision.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (a) sketches that show a horizontal line from the eye and a sight line rising to the top of the tank; (b) learners who note that the string hangs down by gravity; (c) learners who place the angle at the observer's eye and not at the top of the tank. Tally on a checklist how many learners locate the angle correctly. Misconception to note: measuring the angle at the top of the tank or between the sight line and the vertical.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4, learners build a clinometer: (1) tape a straw along the straight edge of a cardboard protractor; (2) push a thread through the small hole at the centre mark and knot it; (3) tie a washer to the free end so the string hangs freely over the scale. Learner 1 holds the clinometer and sights a target through the straw; Learner 2 reads the number where the string crosses the scale; Learner 3 records; Learner 4 checks that the straw is steady. Step A (horizontal check): hold the straw level and look at the far wall at eye height; record where the string hangs (the 90° mark). Step B (tilting up): sight the top of the classroom door frame from 3.0 m away (the eye is at 1.5 m) and record the string position. Learners work out the angle of elevation as the number of degrees between the string and the 90° mark, then compare with the expected value of about 11°. Each learner takes a turn at sighting, reading and recording, and results go in a table: Learner | Scale reading | Angle between string and 90° mark.
framework.teacherMoves: Before building, state safety: 'Scissors handle-first. Straw against your cheek, never pointed at a face. Do not sight at the sun.' Demonstrate the build once while narrating: 'The straw must run exactly along the straight edge. The string must hang from the centre mark.' Use WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after asking 'Where does the string hang when the straw is level, and why is it there?' Mark a floor line at 3.0 m from the door with tape and mark the eye-height point on the wall at 1.5 m. Circulate and ask each group: 'Where is the string when the straw is level? What is that number?' Ask: 'When you tilt the straw up, which way does the string move on the scale?' Prompt groups to record the scale reading before they subtract. If a group gets a value far from 11°, ask: 'Is the straw really on the top of the frame? Is your eye at 1.5 m? Is the string free?' Cold-call 4 groups for their measured angles and write all values on the board; note that they cluster near 11° (some will read 10° to 12°).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured data collection with roles and a class data pool: assigning roles ensures everyone handles the instrument, and pooling all group readings on the board shows learners that real measurements vary slightly but cluster around an expected value. This links directly to the later idea that Wanjiru's and Otieno's readings are to the nearest degree.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (a) the string hangs at 90° when the straw is level; (b) learners subtract the reading from 90° or read the angle from the 90° mark, not the raw scale number; (c) the straw is aligned along the edge and the string moves freely; (d) the group's angle falls in about 10° to 12°. Use a rating scale (Meeting / Approaching / Not yet) and write the groups' names against each. Note any group that reports 79° as the angle of elevation and prompt it to explain the 90° mark.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners use their data to build the explanation. Part 1 (meaning): in groups they complete the definition 'The angle of elevation is the angle ___ the horizontal from the observer's ___ up to the object.' and mark it on a diagram of Wanjiru, the tank and the horizontal line at eye level. Part 2 (complementary angles): they draw the right-angled triangle formed by the protractor's 90° mark, the string and the straw, and explain why the scale reading (for example 79°) and the angle of elevation (11°) are complementary, adding to 90°. Part 3 (tan for height): using the Lesson 4 method, they set up the right-angled triangle for the door frame: the horizontal distance is 3.0 m and the opposite side is the height above eye level. They explain that the door frame is 2.1 m high and the eye is 1.5 m above the floor, so the height above eye level is 0.6 m, and check that tan of the angle is 0.6 ÷ 3.0 = 0.2. They write the general rule: height = (distance × tan angle) + 1.5 m. They then use Wanjiru's values (8 m, 37°) to say what the clinometer would show for her reading: string 37° away from the 90° mark, scale reading 53°. Finally they revise their Predict sketches.
framework.teacherMoves: Ask: 'Where does the angle of elevation begin, at the ground or at the eye? Show me on your diagram.' WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners to place the angle on the board diagram, asking the class for thumbs-up or thumbs-down. Ask: 'Why is the number on the scale not the angle of elevation when the string hangs at 79°?' Take 3 responses and press for the word 'complementary'. Say: 'Remember Lesson 3: complementary angles add to 90°. What is 90° minus 11°?' For Part 3 say: 'This is the same right-angled triangle as in Lesson 4. Which side do we know? Which side do we want? Which ratio connects them?' Cold-call 2 learners to choose tan and give a reason. Tell them: 'We are not working backwards from 0.2 to an angle; the expected angle is about 11° and we simply check against it.' Ask: 'Why do we add 1.5 m at the end of the height?' Take 2 responses. Ask: 'Wanjiru read 37°. Where would the string hang on the scale?' Cold-call 3 learners. Finally say: 'Go back to your Predict sketch. Circle what you got right and fix what you want to change.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with Revisit-the-Prediction: learners state the claim (the angle of elevation is measured from the horizontal at eye level, and the scale reading is its complement), support it with their own clinometer readings, and reason with complementary angles and tan. Connecting Lesson 1 (triangle model), Lesson 3 (complementary angles) and Lesson 4 (setting up tan) shows learners that the new instrument uses ideas they already own.
framework.formativeAssessment: Exit-slip check (3 minutes, individual): (1) 'Define the angle of elevation in one sentence.' (2) 'The string of a clinometer crosses the scale at 53° when the 90° mark is the level position. What is the angle of elevation?' (Expected: 37°.) (3) 'Write the equation for the height of a target 3.0 m away when the angle of elevation is 11°.' (Expected: height = 3.0 × tan 11° + 1.5 m.) Success criteria: at least 80% define the angle from the horizontal at the eye and use the 90° mark correctly. Note learners who read the scale value directly as the angle or leave out the 1.5 m eye height for reteaching.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class Driving Question Board with the columns 'Questions', 'Answered' and 'New understandings'. In groups they write on sticky notes: (1) one question that the clinometer has now answered (for example, 'How did Wanjiru get an angle without climbing?') and move it to 'Answered'; (2) one new understanding (for example, 'The angle of elevation is measured from the horizontal at the eye, and the clinometer reads it between the string and the 90° mark'); (3) one new question that remains (for example, 'How do we measure when the object is below us?' or 'How accurate is a cardboard clinometer outdoors?'). Groups post their notes and the class reads them aloud.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at the DQB. Which of our earlier questions can we move today, and what is your evidence?' WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 4 groups, one per question, to justify moving a note to 'Answered' with evidence from their clinometer. Ask: 'What new question has the clinometer created for you?' Take at least 3 and say that Lesson 6 will take the clinometer outdoors and look at looking down as well as looking up. Ask: 'Which new understanding is most important for finding the height of the tank at Kilimani?' Take 2 responses and have the class vote by show of hands. Tell learners: 'Next lesson, bring your clinometer; we meet the flagpole outside.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a public record of learning: moving questions to 'Answered' with evidence, and adding 'New understandings', shows learners that understanding grows through evidence and that each new tool raises new questions. It keeps the anchoring phenomenon central across lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that: (a) each group's 'Answered' note is supported by evidence from today's clinometer data and not just a statement; (b) at least some new questions point to Lesson 6 ideas (looking down, outdoor accuracy, errors); (c) the 'New understandings' notes use the term 'angle of elevation' correctly. Record which groups' notes show misconceptions, such as treating the scale number as the elevation, for the next lesson's starter.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise their cumulative model (a labelled diagram plus a short written explanation) of how the height of the Kilimani Secondary School water tank can be found without climbing. The new parts of the model are: (1) the horizontal line at eye level (1.5 m above the ground) with the angle of elevation marked between it and the line of sight; (2) the clinometer, with the string, the 90° mark and the scale reading; (3) the right-angled triangle with the horizontal distance as the adjacent side and the height above eye level as the opposite side; (4) the equation height = (distance × tan angle) + 1.5 m. They add an annotation: 'Scale reading = 90° − angle of elevation (complementary angles).' Finally each learner writes 2-3 sentences: 'We can find the height without climbing because ___.' and flags one thing they are still unsure of.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Your model started in Lesson 1 as a triangle with names. Today it gets a real instrument. Add the horizontal at eye level, the angle of elevation, the clinometer and the height rule.' Give 8 minutes of independent work, then 2 minutes of pair review: 'Swap diagrams. Does your partner's angle start at the horizontal at the eye? Is the 1.5 m included?' Circulate and ask: 'Where does the 1.5 m appear in your model?' and 'Which side of your triangle is 6.0 m for Wanjiru's tank?' Cold-call 3 learners to share their sentence, using WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before choosing. Close by saying: 'Next lesson we take the clinometer outside to Kilimani's flagpole and find out how close we can get to the caretaker's tape.' Collect the models to see who still confuses the scale reading with the angle.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision: adding the instrument and the eye-level horizontal to the existing triangle model lets learners see how each lesson's idea fits into one explanation of the phenomenon, and the written 'because' sentence turns the diagram into a causal explanation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Rubric (Meets expectations if all appear): (a) the angle of elevation is drawn from the horizontal at eye level; (b) the clinometer is labelled with the string and the 90° mark; (c) the scale reading is related to the angle by 90° minus the angle; (d) the equation includes the 1.5 m eye height; (e) the explanation sentence refers to the right-angled triangle and the tan ratio. Mark each model as Meeting, Approaching or Not yet, and record which learners to pair with a peer coach for Lesson 6.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect on: (1) Did learners place the angle of elevation at the observer's eye and measure it from the horizontal, or did some still measure from the vertical or the ground? (2) How many groups first reported the raw scale number (for example 79°) as the angle? What helped them link it to complementary angles from Lesson 3? (3) Did the class pool of readings cluster near the expected 11°, and did learners accept that small differences come from reading to the nearest degree? (4) Were the roles (holder, reader, recorder, checker) shared fairly, so that every learner, including quieter ones, handled the clinometer? (5) Which clinometers failed (string sticking, straw crooked), and what materials fix this before Lesson 6? (6) Which DQB questions are ready for Lesson 6, and what extra practice on tan setups is needed for learners who left out the 1.5 m?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We built a clinometer from a cardboard protractor, a straw, a string and a washer. When the straw is level the string hangs at the 90° mark, and when we sighted the top of the classroom door frame (2.1 m high) from 3.0 m the string moved away from 90° by about 11°.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: The angle of elevation is the angle above the horizontal from the observer's eye up to the object. On the clinometer it is the number of degrees between the string and the 90° mark, so the scale reading is 90° minus the angle of elevation (complementary angles). Height = (distance × tan angle) + 1.5 m.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Wanjiru can get an angle for the Kilimani Secondary School water tank without climbing because her clinometer measures the angle of elevation from her eye. That angle, together with her 8 m horizontal distance, gives a right-angled triangle in which tan connects the two, and adding her 1.5 m eye height gives the tank's height.

LESSONS.title: Angle of Depression and Outdoor Measurement: Measuring the Flagpole at Kilimani Secondary School
LESSONS.aresKeywords: angle of depression, angle of elevation, alternate angles, clinometer, field data, horizontal distance, eye height, measurement error, rounding, flagpole, water tank

slo.purpose: Learners extend the angle of elevation to the angle of depression, show that the angle of depression from a high point equals the angle of elevation from the lower point, and use the class-made clinometer outdoors to collect and process real field data (the flagpole), explaining why small errors occur. This moves them closer to confirming the water tank height in Lesson 8.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, the learner should be able to: (1) define angle of elevation and angle of depression and tell them apart; (2) explain why the angle of depression from a high point equals the angle of elevation from the lower point (alternate angles); (3) use height = (distance x tan angle) + 1.5 m to process clinometer data; (4) identify sources of error and explain why results differ slightly from a tape-measured value.
slo.skills: Measuring horizontal distance along level ground with a tape; reading a clinometer (degrees between the string and the 90 degree mark); recording data in a table; setting up and solving tan equations; comparing a calculated value with a tape check and describing the error; collaborating in groups of 4. NGSS practices: Planning and Carrying Out Investigations; Analyzing and Interpreting Data; Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking.
slo.attitudes: Appreciate the use of trigonometry in real-life situations (KICD SLO e); show care and honesty when recording measurements, including readings that do not match expectations; value teamwork and careful use of locally made instruments.
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 5 gave learners the clinometer and the angle of elevation. Lesson 4 gave them the skill of solving for sides. In Lesson 6 they go outdoors for the first time to measure a real structure (the flagpole, 9.0 m), meet the angle of depression, and see that real measurements carry small errors. This prepares them for Lesson 7 (multi-step problems and error analysis) and for Lesson 8, where clinometer results are reconciled with the water tank at Kilimani Secondary School, Nakuru. Learners should leave knowing a method that gave 9.1 m for a 9.0 m pole can be trusted, and that it is the same method that gave 7.5 m for the tank.
slo.safetyNotes: Keep learners on level, open ground away from roads and drains. Never sight toward the sun. Nobody climbs the flagpole, the tank tower or the veranda rails. Tape measures are not swung or thrown. Washers on strings are held, not swung. Learners stay within sight of Madam Achieng; groups are of 4 with set roles. The veranda task is done from a safe standing position behind the rail, with no leaning over.

LESSONS.overview: Madam Achieng opens by reminding the class of the tank puzzle: Wanjiru (8 m, 37 degrees) and Otieno (10 m, 31 degrees) never climbed the tower, yet both got the same height. Learners predict what happens when the observer is HIGH and looks DOWN at a marker on the ground, and whether that angle is related to the angle from the ground looking up. They then make observations in two parts. Part A (veranda): from an eye level 3.0 m above the ground, they sight a ground marker 4.0 m from the veranda base and find the angle of depression is 37 degrees, and check it with tan 37 degrees = 0.7536 and 4.0 x 0.7536 = 3.01 m, about 3.0 m. Part B (field): in groups of 4 they use their clinometers to measure the school flagpole. Sample group Amani stands 15 m from the base, reads 27 degrees, and calculates 15 x tan 27 degrees + 1.5 = 7.64 + 1.5 = 9.1 m, against Mr. Kamau's tape value of 9.0 m, an error of 0.1 m caused by reading to the nearest degree. In the Explain phase learners use alternate angles to explain depression equals elevation, and analyse why groups' results vary slightly. The DQB and model are updated: the method works outdoors, and answers carry small errors.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the tank scenario (Wanjiru at 8 m reading 37 degrees, Otieno at 10 m reading 31 degrees). Madam Achieng sketches a person on the Kilimani veranda looking DOWN at a stone on the ground, then a second person standing at the stone looking UP at the veranda rail. Individually, in notebooks, learners write: (1) a prediction about how the two angles are related (bigger, smaller, equal, or no relationship) with a reason; (2) a prediction of how close the group's flagpole calculation will be to the real height and why it may not be exact. They draw a quick sketch showing where the angle is measured from. They then share with a partner and commit to one prediction on a sticky note for the class chart.
framework.teacherMoves: Draw the veranda sketch and say: 'Last lesson you looked UP with your clinometer. Today someone stands high and looks DOWN. Is the angle going to be the same, or different?' Give silent WAIT TIME of 15 seconds before anyone writes. Say: 'Write your prediction and one reason. There is no wrong answer yet.' Circulate and cold-call 4 learners with different predictions (for example one saying equal, one saying bigger, one saying not related). Ask: 'What made you think that?' Record each prediction as a tally on the board without judging. Then ask: 'If our method gave the tank height without climbing it, how close do you think we will get to the flagpole when we check with Mr. Kamau's tape? Exact? Within 1 m? Within 0.1 m?' WAIT TIME 10 seconds. Tell learners we will revisit these predictions in the Explain phase.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction with reasoning (Predict-Observe-Explain): committing to a prediction and a reason in writing, before seeing evidence, exposes learners' initial ideas about angles measured from high and low points. Because the predictions are recorded publicly, learners feel the need for evidence and notice later when the data support or contradict them.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that at least 80% of learners wrote a prediction with a reason. Observable indicators: (1) the sketch places the angle at the observer's eye, measured from the horizontal; (2) learners use the words elevation, depression or horizontal; (3) learners give an idea about error or rounding. Note learners who measure the angle from the vertical or from the sloping line to the ground, and plan to address this in the Observe phase. Tally predictions on the board: equal / bigger / smaller / no relation.

framework.learnerExperience: Part A, veranda (about 20 minutes): groups of 4 meet at the veranda. Madam Achieng marks eye level at 3.0 m above the ground and places a ground marker 4.0 m from the base of the veranda. Learners sight the marker with the clinometer held to the eye, with the straw pointing down at the marker, and observe that the string reads against the protractor, with the angle of depression measured from the horizontal line of sight (the 90 degree mark) down to the line of sight. They find about 37 degrees. They check with tan 37 degrees = 0.7536 and 4.0 x 0.7536 = 3.01 m, about 3.0 m. A learner then stands at the marker and sights up to the veranda rail at the eye-level mark, reading an elevation also about 37 degrees. Part B, flagpole (about 40 minutes): each group of 4 gets roles: sighter, string-reader, tape-holder, recorder. They measure a horizontal distance on level ground from the base of the flagpole (Group Amani uses 15 m), sight the top, and record the angle. Group Amani reads 27 degrees. They record data in a table: distance, angle, tan of angle, distance x tan, plus 1.5 m eye height, calculated height. Group Amani: 15 x 0.5095 = 7.64; 7.64 + 1.5 = 9.1 m. Each learner in the group takes a turn sighting, and groups repeat the reading and note any differences. Back in class, Mr. Kamau's tape value of 9.0 m is shown for comparison.
framework.teacherMoves: At the veranda, say: 'The straw must point at the marker. Where is the horizontal? Show me with your hand.' Before anyone reads, give WAIT TIME of 10 seconds for learners to locate the 90 degree mark. Cold-call 3 learners: 'Where do you start measuring the angle from?' (from the horizontal, not the ground). Ask: 'What do you notice about the angle when the observer is on the ground looking up at the rail, compared with looking down from the veranda?' WAIT TIME 10 seconds. Outdoors, circulate and prompt: 'Is the tape on level ground? Is your 15 m measured to the base, not to the shadow of the pole?' Check that the clinometer is held at eye level and the reader waits for the washer to settle. Say: 'Take the reading twice. If the two readings differ by 1 degree, record both.' Ask each recorder: 'Show me your table. What do you do with the 1.5 m?' Remind: 'Safe distances, no one near the flagpole ropes.' Back in class, show the sample results and Mr. Kamau's 9.0 m, and ask: 'The tape says 9.0 m. We got 9.1 m. Is that a failure?' WAIT TIME 15 seconds.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured data collection with role rotation and data table (Planning and Carrying Out Investigations): organising raw readings into a table of distance, angle, tan and height makes patterns and spread visible. Using the veranda case first lets learners see depression and elevation as a pair before they handle noisy outdoor data.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) learners hold the clinometer at eye level and read the angle between the string and the 90 degree mark; (2) tape measured along level ground to the base; (3) recorder completes all table columns with the 1.5 m eye height added; (4) depression reading at the veranda is within about 2 degrees of 37 degrees; (5) calculations give a flagpole height within about 0.5 m of 9.0 m. Use a checklist with 3 levels: independent, with prompts, needs support. Ask 2 groups to show their tables and explain why they added 1.5 m.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners complete three sense-making tasks. (1) Explain the equality of angles: using the veranda sketch, they draw the horizontal line through the high eye and the horizontal line through the ground eye, and the line of sight between them. They label the angle of depression (below the upper horizontal) and the angle of elevation (above the lower horizontal) and use alternate angles between parallel lines to explain why both are 37 degrees. They add the right-angled triangle with opposite 3.0 m and adjacent 4.0 m and show that tan 37 degrees = 0.7536 gives 4.0 x 0.7536 = 3.01 m, about 3.0 m. (2) Interpret the flagpole result: Group Amani's 9.1 m versus 9.0 m. They list possible reasons for the 0.1 m error (reading the angle to the nearest degree, string swinging, slight tilt of the straw, tape not exactly straight, level of ground, eye height not exactly 1.5 m) and decide which is the main one. They check how much 1 degree changes the answer: 15 x tan 27 degrees = 7.64 m versus 15 x tan 28 degrees = 15 x 0.5317 = 7.98 m, which is a change of 0.3 m. (3) Return to the Predict phase and revise their predictions in a different colour of pen. They link the flagpole results to the tank: Wanjiru's and Otieno's 7.5 m, which differ only through rounding.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Draw two horizontal lines, one at the veranda eye level and one at your eye on the ground. What is true about them?' (parallel). WAIT TIME 15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners: 'Which angles are equal, and why?' Introduce the term alternate angles if no one uses it. Ask: 'Which would be easier to measure in real life, depression from the roof or elevation from the ground? Why?' Then say: 'Group Amani got 9.1 m and the tape says 9.0 m. Who can tell me what 0.1 m means in a 9 m pole?' Cold-call 2 learners. Challenge: 'If they had read 28 degrees instead of 27, what would the height be?' Give 10 seconds, then show the calculation: 15 x 0.5317 = 7.98, plus 1.5 = 9.5 m. Ask: 'So what does one degree of reading error do to our answer?' Press for evidence: 'What in the data tells you that?' Avoid giving the answer first. Then ask: 'What does this say about how confident we can be about the tank height of 7.5 m?' WAIT TIME 10 seconds. Ask 4 learners to read out their revised predictions.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with sensitivity testing: learners claim that depression equals elevation and back it with the veranda measurements and alternate-angle geometry. They also test how a 1 degree change affects the answer, which gives them evidence-based reasoning about error instead of treating 0.1 m as a mistake.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) a diagram with two parallel horizontals, correctly labelled depression and elevation; (2) correct use of alternate angles in the explanation; (3) correct calculation 15 x 0.5095 + 1.5 = 9.1 m and the error stated as 0.1 m; (4) at least two valid sources of error, with reading to the nearest degree named as the main one; (5) revised predictions that refer to the data. Common misconception to listen for: measuring the angle of depression from the vertical or from the ground. Use a 3-question exit slip: (a) Define angle of depression. (b) If the depression from a roof is 40 degrees, what is the elevation from the ground? (c) Give one reason why a calculated height may differ slightly from a tape measurement.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class Driving Question Board with three columns: 'Questions', 'Answered' and 'New understandings'. In groups they move earlier questions to 'Answered' where the evidence supports it (for example, 'Can we find a height without climbing?' and 'Does the angle depend on where you stand?'). They write at least one new understanding on a sticky note, such as 'Angle of depression from a high point = angle of elevation from the lower point', 'Field readings give answers that are close, not exact (flagpole 9.1 m vs 9.0 m)', and 'One degree of error changes the flagpole height by about 0.3 m'. They then post new questions, such as 'How do we reduce error?', 'Can we use sin and cos for slanted lengths too, like a rafter or a ramp?', and 'Will the clinometer give 7.5 m for the tank?'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Go to the DQB with your group. Which questions can we now move to Answered? Show me the evidence from today.' Give 2 minutes of silent reading, then WAIT TIME 10 seconds. Cold-call 3 groups: 'Which question are you moving, and what is your evidence?' Ask the class: 'Do we agree?' Then say: 'Each group write ONE new question that today's measuring made you wonder about.' Collect at least 4 questions. Point out to learners that the question about slanted lengths will be explored in the next lesson and that the tank confirmation is coming in Lesson 8. Ask: 'Which new question would help us improve our flagpole result?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Public question tracking (DQB): moving questions between columns and adding new understandings makes progress visible and keeps the driving question (how to find a height or distance without measuring it directly) alive. Writing questions that arise from error encourages learners to treat uncertainty as something to investigate.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) each group moves at least one question and cites specific evidence from today; (2) new understandings are stated accurately, using the terms depression, elevation and error; (3) new questions are testable and linked to the tank, such as reducing error or using sin and cos; (4) learners listen and respond to other groups' notes. Record which groups wrote questions about error or accuracy to help plan Lesson 7.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners update their class model of how to find the tank height without climbing it. In groups they redraw the model diagram so it now includes: (a) the tank tower with the observer on level ground, horizontal distance, eye height 1.5 m, angle of elevation; (b) a second sketch with the observer on a high point looking down, showing that depression equals elevation; (c) a short note on the method: height = (distance x tan angle) + 1.5 m, using the Group Amani flagpole as a worked check (15 x tan 27 degrees + 1.5 = 9.1 m, tape 9.0 m); and (d) an 'error box' that lists the sources of error and states that angles are read to the nearest degree. They also write a short caption explaining how the flagpole result makes them more confident in the tank method used by Wanjiru (8 m, 37 degrees) and Otieno (10 m, 31 degrees), who both got 7.5 m.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Your model now needs to explain two new things: what happens when we look down, and why real measurements are a little off. Add them.' Circulate and ask each group: 'Where in your model does the 1.5 m come in? Where is the horizontal?' WAIT TIME 10 seconds before follow-ups. Cold-call 3 groups to explain their error box. Prompt: 'Is 0.1 m in 9.0 m a big error? How could we check?' (about 1%). Encourage each group to add one limit: 'Where might your model not work?' (for example, sloping ground, a tape not level). Close by asking, 'What do you expect to happen when we compare our clinometer results with Mr. Kamau's tape value for the tank?' and tell them that comparison happens in Lesson 8. Collect model drawings for a gallery walk next lesson.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision: adding depression, field data and error to the existing tank model shows how scientific and mathematical models grow with new evidence. Stating limits and error ranges helps learners see a model as a tool whose accuracy can be judged.
framework.formativeAssessment: Use a 4-point checklist: (1) diagram has labelled horizontal, line of sight, angle and 1.5 m eye height; (2) depression = elevation is shown using alternate angles; (3) method formula is correct and the flagpole check (9.1 m vs 9.0 m) is cited; (4) the error box names at least two sources and states that rounding to the nearest degree is the main one. Note groups that include a limit of the model. Use this evidence to plan Lesson 7 support for learners who confuse the angle's reference line.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Before the lesson: Did you check that the ground by the flagpole is level and that you have at least one tape measure of 15 m or more per two groups? Have the clinometers been checked so that the string hangs freely and the straw is firmly taped? During the lesson: Which learners found the 90 degree mark and horizontal difficult? Did learners treat the 0.1 m difference as a failure or as expected error? Did anyone ask whether the equality of depression and elevation works for any angle (carry this to the DQB)? After the lesson: Review the exit slips. Which learners can state the definition of depression and apply alternate angles? Which groups got heights more than 0.5 m from 9.0 m, and do they need to repeat the reading? Plan for Lesson 7 which will use sin, cos and tan for multi-step slant-length problems, and for Lesson 8 where learners will reconcile their clinometer data with the tank at Kilimani Secondary School.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: What did we observe? Record the veranda results (eye level 3.0 m, marker 4.0 m from the base, angle of depression about 37 degrees, with 4.0 x tan 37 degrees = 3.01 m, about 3.0 m) and our flagpole data (distance, clinometer angle, calculated height, tape value 9.0 m).
summaryTablePrompt.learned: What did we learn? Write what the angle of depression is, how it relates to the angle of elevation from the lower point (alternate angles), and how field data compare with the tape measurement (for Group Amani: 15 m, 27 degrees, 9.1 m versus 9.0 m).
summaryTablePrompt.explained: How does this help explain the phenomenon? Explain, in your own words, how the height of the water tank can be found without climbing it, why the answers are close to the real height but not exact, and what causes the small error when we read angles to the nearest degree.
