LESSONS.title: Multi-Step Problems and Error Analysis: Which Ratio Do I Choose?
LESSONS.aresKeywords: choosing sin cos tan, slant length, vertical height, angle of elevation, angle of depression, error analysis, eye height, DEG mode, checking predictions, Kilimani water tank

slo.purpose: Learners choose sin, cos or tan in unfamiliar multi-step elevation and depression contexts (slant lengths and vertical heights), spot and correct typical errors, and evaluate their Lesson 1 predictions about the Kilimani water tank.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the sub strand, the learner should be able to: b) determine the sine, cosine and tangent of acute angles in a right-angled triangle; d) apply trigonometric ratios to angles of elevation and depression. In this lesson: the choice of ratio depends on which side is known and which is wanted (opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse relative to the angle). Slant lengths often need sin or cos, while vertical heights from a horizontal distance need tan. Eye height of 1.5 m is added only when the sighting is made from eye level.
slo.skills: Identify the right-angled triangle in a word problem and draw a labelled sketch; name opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse from the given angle; choose sin, cos or tan; set up and solve the equation; check DEG mode; state answers with units and appropriate rounding; critique worked solutions to find errors (wrong ratio, calculator in RAD mode, forgetting the 1.5 m eye height, mixing up the angle); evaluate earlier predictions against evidence. NGSS-aligned practices: Analyzing and Interpreting Data, Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking, Engaging in Argument from Evidence, Constructing Explanations.
slo.attitudes: Core competency: Self-efficacy: the learner makes observations and establishes relationships between the ratios. Learning to learn: the learner learns collaboratively when checking each other's work. Value: Love: the learner shows a caring attitude to others when giving feedback on mistakes. PCI: Self-esteem: the learner treats errors as steps in learning.
slo.keyInquiry: Why is trigonometry important? (KICD key inquiry question)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 4, 5 and 6 taught learners to set up equations for unknown sides, to read the clinometer and to understand elevation, depression and field errors. Lesson 7 stretches those skills to unfamiliar contexts, checks that learners can choose the right ratio, and uses Lesson 1 predictions to show how much the class has learned. It prepares learners for Lesson 8, where they write the full tank solution and reconcile it with Mr. Kamau's tape check.
slo.safetyNotes: This lesson is indoors and desk-based. No climbing is needed. Learners should keep walkways clear and not stand on desks or chairs to sight objects. Calculators should be handled with care, and learners should share them fairly.

LESSONS.overview: Madam Achieng opens with the question: 'Wanjiru and Otieno found the tank height using tan. Would tan work for every problem?' Learners first recall their Lesson 1 predictions about how to find the tank height without climbing. They then attempt three unfamiliar problems: a Rift Valley farmer sighting a cliff (tan), a Watamu diver's weighted line (sin), and a Nairobi ramp (sin). In the Observe phase they collect evidence by solving and sorting problems into 'known side / wanted side' ratio choices. In the Explain phase they critique four worked solutions containing typical errors, including a calculator in the wrong mode and a forgotten eye height, and build a ratio-choice decision guide. They then revisit Lesson 1 predictions, add to the Driving Question Board (DQB), and revise the class model so that it includes how to choose the ratio and how to detect errors. This links directly to the phenomenon: Wanjiru at 8 m and 37° and Otieno at 10 m and 31° both obtain 7.5 m using height = distance x tan(angle) + 1.5 m, and the same decision skills will be needed in Lesson 8.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners take out their Lesson 1 prediction sheets about how to find the height of the Kilimani Secondary School water tank without climbing it. Individually (3 minutes), they reread and mark each idea with a tick (still holds), a question mark (unsure) or a cross (needs revising). Then they see this prompt on the board: 'A diver at Watamu lets out a weighted line 12 m long and it makes 50 degrees with the horizontal water surface. We know the angle and the line length (the slanted side). Which ratio will give the depth, sin, cos or tan? Why?' Learners write a prediction with a short reason and sketch a quick triangle. They then pair up and compare their choices.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take out your Lesson 1 predictions. Read them silently and mark each one: tick, question mark or cross.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before circulating. Draw the Watamu scenario on the board without labelling sides and say: 'Before we calculate anything, predict: which ratio, and why? Write your reason in one sentence.' Give 10-15 seconds of WAIT TIME. Cold-call 3 learners for different predictions and record every prediction on the board without judging. Ask: 'Does anyone have a different idea? What in the problem makes you choose that ratio?' Remind learners: 'Wanjiru's tank used tan. Is this the same type of problem?' Do not confirm yet; say: 'We will test these predictions with evidence today.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction with justification (Predict-Observe-Explain). Writing a reason before calculation exposes the ideas learners hold about ratio choice, such as always using tan because the tank used tan. Revisiting Lesson 1 predictions shows how their thinking has changed since the start of the unit.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check prediction sheets for (a) whether learners name the known and wanted sides in their reasoning, (b) whether any learner insists that tan is always the answer, (c) whether learners can sketch the right-angled triangle correctly. Tally on the board how many chose sin, cos or tan. Note learners who cannot start a sketch for follow-up support.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4, learners solve three problems drawn from Kenyan contexts. They draw a labelled triangle for each, mark the angle theta, label hypotenuse, opposite and adjacent, and choose and justify a ratio. (a) A Rift Valley farmer stands 150 m from the base of a cliff and measures an angle of elevation of 40 degrees (eye height ignored). Find the cliff height. (b) A Watamu diver's weighted line is 12 m long and makes 50 degrees with the horizontal surface. Find the depth. (c) A Nairobi ramp is 5 m long along the slope and rises at 8 degrees to the horizontal. Find the vertical rise. They confirm calculators are in DEG mode, calculate, and record in a table: Problem | Known side | Wanted side | Ratio chosen | Working | Answer. Expected results: (a) 150 x tan 40 = 150 x 0.8391 = 125.9 m, about 126 m; (b) 12 x sin 50 = 12 x 0.7660 = 9.2 m; (c) 5 x sin 8 = 5 x 0.1392 = 0.70 m (0.7 m). They then compare answers with another group and resolve any disagreements, finally checking whether each answer is reasonable (for example, the ramp rise cannot be larger than the 5 m slope length, and the depth cannot exceed 12 m).
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute the problem sheet and ruled tables. Say: 'For each problem, draw the triangle first. Label the three sides from the angle before you pick a ratio.' Circulate and ask: 'Which side do you know? Which side do you want? Where is the right angle?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question before giving any hint. Check that calculators show DEG. If a group says 'I used tan for the ramp', ask: 'Is the 5 m the opposite, adjacent or hypotenuse side?' Do not hand over the answer. After 15 minutes, cold-call 3 groups, one per problem, to share their ratio choice and answer. Ask the class: 'Is the answer reasonable? Could the ramp rise be more than 5 m?' Record answers on the board and the ratio choices in a class table. Ask: 'What pattern do you notice between the sides we know and the ratio we picked?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data table and pattern-seeking. Recording known side, wanted side and ratio for several problems lets learners see a pattern: opposite and adjacent give tan, opposite and hypotenuse give sin, adjacent and hypotenuse give cos. The reasonableness check builds number sense and ties to the sources of error from Lesson 6.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: correctly labelled triangles; ratio choice supported by naming the two sides; answers of about 126 m, 9.2 m and 0.7 m within rounding; DEG mode checked; units written. Use a checklist during circulation. Learners who label the hypotenuse incorrectly or choose a ratio without naming sides need a re-teach of side naming from Lesson 1 using a small sketch.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners now critique four worked solutions written by 'fictional classmates' and find the error in each. Error 1: In the cliff problem, 'Mwende' used 150 x sin 40 = 96.4 m (wrong ratio: she had opposite and adjacent, so tan was needed). Error 2: 'Baraka' calculated 12 x sin 50 and got 0.0 (approximately 0.8) because his calculator was in RAD mode (wrong mode). Error 3: 'Zawadi' calculated the Kilimani tank height as 8 x tan 37 = 6.03 m and said this was the tank height, forgetting to add the 1.5 m eye height (the answer should be 7.5 m). Error 4: 'Kiprop' used the angle 8 degrees in the ramp problem but put the angle at the wrong end, using cos 8 and getting 4.95 m (wrong ratio or wrong angle position). Groups write a corrected solution and a one-sentence tip for avoiding that error. The class then builds a Ratio Choice Decision Guide poster: (1) Draw and label the triangle. (2) Name the known side and the wanted side. (3) Choose the ratio linking them. (4) Check DEG mode. (5) Add the 1.5 m eye height if the angle was measured from eye level. (6) Check that the answer is reasonable. Finally they explain, in two sentences, why Wanjiru and Otieno both get 7.5 m even though their angles differ (the ratio opposite divided by adjacent depends only on the angle, so the closer learner has a larger angle, and the calculation compensates).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Four students at another school made mistakes. Your job is to be the detective. Find the error, fix it and write a tip.' Give 10-15 seconds of WAIT TIME after posing each error. Cold-call 4 learners, one per error, to explain what went wrong. Probe: 'How could you have caught that without knowing the right answer?' For Error 3, ask: 'Where does Wanjiru's eye sit above the ground? Where is the top of the tank measured from?' Ask: 'Is it a problem to make mistakes?' and affirm: 'Finding errors is how mathematicians improve.' Guide the class to create the decision guide; write each step as learners offer it, and ask 2 learners to challenge any unclear step. Use the question: 'Wanjiru stands 8 m away and Otieno 10 m away. Why do their angles differ but the height does not?' and allow 10-15 seconds of WAIT TIME before taking 3 responses.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Error analysis and consensus model building. Diagnosing other people's mistakes lets learners recognise their own typical errors without embarrassment. Building a shared decision guide turns separate fixes into a transferable procedure, and explaining why both learners obtain 7.5 m links the procedure to the underlying idea that the ratio depends on the angle only.
framework.formativeAssessment: Listen for learners who (a) correctly identify wrong ratio, RAD mode, missing eye height and misplaced angle; (b) state the corrected ratio with sides named; (c) mention that the 1.5 m is added only when the angle is measured from eye level; (d) explain the two-learner consistency using the angle-ratio idea. Use a thumbs-up self-check: 'How confident are you in choosing the ratio?' (up, sideways, down) and note learners who need additional practice.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the DQB, which has the columns 'Questions', 'Answered' and 'New understandings'. In groups they read the questions posted since Lesson 1 and decide which ones can now be moved to 'Answered', such as 'Which side do we use?', 'Does the size of the triangle matter?' and 'How do we know which ratio to use?'. They write evidence from today (for example, the Watamu, cliff and ramp problems) on sticky notes. They then write new understandings, such as 'The ratio depends on the known side and the wanted side' and 'Always check DEG mode and eye height'. Finally each group adds one new question for Lesson 8, for example 'How close will our clinometer answer be to Mr. Kamau's measured value?' or 'How can we show the full solution clearly?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at our DQB. Which questions can we answer now? Show me the evidence from today.' Give 10-15 seconds of WAIT TIME before groups move any note. Cold-call 3 groups to justify why a question has moved to 'Answered' and ask the class: 'Do you agree? What evidence supports that?' If a group cannot give evidence, keep the note in 'Questions'. Prompt: 'What new question do we have now that we did not have in Lesson 1?' Ask each group to post exactly one new question. Highlight a question about accuracy and say: 'Lesson 8 will help us test this when we compare with Mr. Kamau's tape check.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a public record of progress. Moving questions to 'Answered' only with evidence encourages claim-evidence reasoning, and new questions show how understanding has deepened and keep the driving question alive.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that questions moved to 'Answered' are supported by evidence from the lesson, that 'New understandings' use correct language (opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse, sin, cos, tan), and that new questions point to accuracy and complete solutions. Observe whether all group members contribute.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit the class model for the phenomenon 'How tall is the water tank without climbing it?' and the Lesson 1 predictions. Each learner writes an Evaluation of Predictions note: what my original prediction said, what evidence supports or contradicts it, and how I would change it. They then add to the group model: a labelled diagram of the Kilimani tank tower with Wanjiru at 8 m and 37 degrees and Otieno at 10 m and 31 degrees, the 1.5 m eye height, the equation height = distance x tan(angle) + 1.5 m, and the decision guide steps. They also add a 'Watch out' box listing four typical errors (wrong ratio, RAD mode, no eye height, wrong angle position). Learners complete a short exit task: a surveyor on the Thika Superhighway stands 20 m from the base of a pylon and measures an elevation of 35 degrees; decide the ratio and write the first line of the equation only (tan 35 = h divided by 20). Groups share their updated models in a gallery walk and leave one comment on another group's model.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open your Lesson 1 prediction. Using today's evidence, how would you change it? Write what stays, what changes and why.' Give 10-15 seconds of WAIT TIME before learners start writing. Circulate and ask: 'Which part of your first prediction was closest to the method Wanjiru and Otieno used?' For the model, ask: 'Where does 1.5 m appear in your diagram? Why is it there?' Cold-call 3 learners for their exit task ratio choice. For the gallery walk, say: 'Leave one comment that begins with: I noticed that...' Close by saying: 'In Lesson 8 you will write the full solution and compare it with Mr. Kamau's tape check of the tank.' Do not reveal the tape value.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision with prediction evaluation. Comparing Lesson 1 predictions with current understanding shows learners their conceptual change and strengthens metacognition. Adding the error box makes the model more complete and usable.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for evaluation notes that cite evidence (for example, ratios depend on angle, tan links opposite and adjacent), models that include correct labelling and the 1.5 m eye height, and exit task answers that choose tan with correct sides. Use a simple 3-level rubric: complete (all four elements), developing (two or three), beginning (one or none). Learners at 'beginning' get targeted support in Lesson 8.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: (1) How many learners correctly named the known and wanted sides before choosing a ratio? (2) Which error was most common in the critique task, and what does that say about earlier lessons? (3) Did learners hold the idea that tan is always used because of the tank problem, and did the Watamu and ramp problems change it? (4) Did learners connect Lesson 1 predictions to evidence with specific reasons? (5) Which learners were over-reliant on peers during the group tasks, and how can they be supported before Lesson 8? (6) Were calculators shared fairly and were all in DEG mode? Plan extra practice or a short revision of side naming for learners who still struggle.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: What did we observe? Record the three problems (Rift Valley cliff, Watamu diver, Nairobi ramp): the known side, the wanted side, the ratio we chose, and our answers (about 126 m, 9.2 m and 0.7 m). Add the four errors found in the critique task.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: What did we learn? Write how to choose sin, cos or tan from the known and wanted sides, when to add the 1.5 m eye height, why DEG mode matters, and how our Lesson 1 predictions have changed.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: How does this help explain the phenomenon? Explain in your own words why Wanjiru (8 m, 37 degrees) and Otieno (10 m, 31 degrees) both get a tank height of 7.5 m, and how choosing the correct ratio and avoiding common errors lets us find the height of the water tank without climbing it.

reading.title: Trigonometry Word Problems: Helicopter Angle of Depression Rescue (PLIX)
Angles of Elevation and Depression Practice

LESSONS.title: Solving the Water Tank Problem: Final Explanation
LESSONS.aresKeywords: water tank, tangent, angle of elevation, clinometer, eye height, consistency check, rounding error, final explanation, Kilimani Secondary School, Mr. Kamau

slo.purpose: To bring together everything learned in Lessons 1-7 so that learners can write a complete labelled diagram and written solution for the water-tank problem, reconcile their own clinometer results with Mr. Kamau's tape-measured height, and give a final explanation of how trigonometry lets us find heights and distances without measuring them directly.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (a) apply trigonometric ratios to angles of elevation and depression; (b) identify the right-angled triangle in relation to a particular angle (opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse); (c) determine the sine, cosine and tangent of acute angles in a right-angled triangle; (d) recognise the use of trigonometry in real-life situations. Learners will explain that opposite ÷ adjacent depends only on the angle, not the size of the triangle, which is why Wanjiru (8 m, 37°) and Otieno (10 m, 31°) both get 7.5 m.
slo.skills: Constructing a complete labelled diagram; selecting a ratio from the known and wanted sides; setting up and solving height = (distance x tan angle) + 1.5 m; stating answers to 1 d.p. with units; evaluating accuracy and rounding error; constructing an evidence-based written explanation and revising a model (NGSS: constructing explanations, developing and using models, engaging in argument from evidence, analysing and interpreting data).
slo.attitudes: Self-efficacy as learners see they can find a height they cannot climb; love and care for peers when they use the clinometer together and give kind, specific feedback; appreciation of trigonometry in surveying, engineering and forestry; self-esteem from presenting a final solution. KICD core competencies: self-efficacy and learning to learn. Value: love. PCI: self-esteem.
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the culmination of the storyline. In Lesson 1 learners could only predict how to find the tank height. They then derived sin, cos and tan (L2), related complementary angles (L3), solved for unknown sides (L4), built and read a clinometer (L5), collected field data and met errors (L6), and solved multi-step problems (L7). In Lesson 8 they use all of this to write the final explanation, reveal Mr. Kamau's tape value of 7.5 m, and close the explanatory loop.
slo.safetyNotes: Any outdoor re-check of the flagpole or tank data stays on level ground, away from the tank tower base, steel frame and any ladder. Learners never climb the tower or frame. Clinometers are used only for sighting the object: learners must never sight at the sun. Move in pairs, keep within the teacher's sight and keep tape measures and strings from tangling at feet.

LESSONS.overview: Madam Achieng opens with the question learners could not answer in Lesson 1: how tall is the water tank at Kilimani Secondary School, Nakuru, if nobody can climb it? Learners first make a final prediction of the tank height from Wanjiru's and Otieno's data and compare it with their Lesson 1 predictions. They then write a complete solution (diagram, triangle, ratio, calculation, units, explanation) for Wanjiru (8 m, 37°) and Otieno (10 m, 31°), checking that both give 7.5 m. Mr. Kamau's tape check of 7.5 m is revealed. Learners use the Group Amani flagpole example (9.1 m against 9.0 m) to discuss why small differences arise from reading angles to the nearest degree. They then complete the Driving Question Board, compare their Lesson 1 model with a final model, and write the Final Explanation answering the driving question and the key inquiry question: Why is trigonometry important?

framework.learnerExperience: Learners open their Lesson 1 notebook pages and re-read their first prediction for the tank height. Individually (3 minutes) they write a new, final prediction on a sticky note: 'Wanjiru stands 8 m from the tower and reads 37°. Her eye is 1.5 m above the ground. I predict the top of the tank is ___ m high because ___.' They also predict whether Otieno (10 m, 31°) will get the same height as Wanjiru, and why a smaller angle at a greater distance could still give the same answer. They place the notes in a 'Prediction wall' next to their Lesson 1 notes.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Last time, we could only guess. Today, you have all the tools. Before we calculate, I want your best prediction, and I want a reason.' Draw the tower, Wanjiru and Otieno on the board with distances and angles only, not the answer. Ask: 'Who will get the larger angle, Wanjiru or Otieno? Why?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before taking any answer. Cold-call 4 learners to share their prediction and reason. Ask 2 of them: 'What changed from your Lesson 1 prediction?' Do not say whether any prediction is right. Record the range of predictions on the board.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction revisited (Predict-Observe-Explain). Learners compare their present thinking with their Lesson 1 thinking, making their own progress visible and giving them a stake in finding out whether their reasoning holds. Naming the reason behind each prediction exposes whether learners rely on ratio ideas or on guessing.
framework.formativeAssessment: Listen for predictions that mention tan, opposite and adjacent, or the idea that a closer observer sees a larger angle. Look for numbers in a sensible range (above 1.5 m and below about 15 m). Note learners who still say they must measure the tank directly or climb it. Tick on a class list who gives a ratio-based reason versus a guess.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners gather evidence from the full anchor data. (1) In pairs they read Wanjiru's and Otieno's data cards: Wanjiru 8 m, 37°; Otieno 10 m, 31°; eye height 1.5 m for each. (2) Each pair draws a large labelled diagram for each learner on a plain page or graph paper: tower, level ground, observer, 1.5 m eye height, horizontal line at eye level, angle θ at the eye, and the sides labelled opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse. (3) They compute: tan 37° = 0.7536; 8 x 0.7536 = 6.03 m above eye level; 6.03 + 1.5 = 7.53 m, about 7.5 m. Then tan 31° = 0.6009; 10 x 0.6009 = 6.01 m; 6.01 + 1.5 = 7.51 m, about 7.5 m. Calculators are in DEG mode. (4) Pairs swap and peer-check using a checklist: diagram labelled? correct triangle? tan chosen and why? units? eye height added? (5) Mr. Kamau's tape result is revealed: the top of the tank is 7.5 m. (6) Group Amani's flagpole data (15 m, 27°, 15 x 0.5095 + 1.5 = 9.1 m against the caretaker's 9.0 m) is displayed for comparison.
framework.teacherMoves: Hand out data cards and say: 'Draw first, calculate second. If I cannot see your triangle, I cannot see your thinking.' Circulate and ask: 'Which side is opposite your angle? Which side do you know? Why tan and not sin?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after each question. Check calculators are in DEG mode: ask 3 pairs to show you tan 37° = 0.7536. Watch for common slips: forgetting the 1.5 m eye height, using 7.53 as the distance, or using sin instead of tan. Prompt: 'Is 6.03 m the height of the tank or the height above your eye?' After peer checking, hold the tape result back for 10 seconds of silence, then say: 'Mr. Kamau climbed the tower during maintenance and measured with a tape. He got 7.5 metres.' Ask 3 cold-called learners: 'How does 7.53 compare with 7.5? How does 7.51 compare?' Then show the flagpole example: 'Group Amani calculated 9.1 m. Mr. Kamau's tape said 9.0 m. Where could the 0.1 m come from?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Evidence-based consistency check and structured peer review. Two different measurements (different distance, different angle) converging on one height, confirmed by an independent tape measurement, gives learners direct evidence that the method works. The checklist makes the five solution steps explicit so learners internalise the structure of a complete written solution.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check diagrams: eye-level horizontal drawn, 1.5 m shown separately from 6.0 m, angle at the eye (not at the tank), sides correctly labelled. Check working: tan chosen with reasoning, tan values to 4 d.p., 8 x 0.7536 = 6.03, + 1.5 = 7.53, rounded to 7.5 m with units. Ask pairs to state in one sentence why Otieno and Wanjiru agree. Record how many pairs correctly add 1.5 m on the first attempt and revisit those who do not.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in groups of 4 to write a Complete Written Solution for the water tank on a poster or in their books, following the five steps: (1) Labelled diagram; (2) Identify the triangle and the known and wanted sides relative to θ; (3) Choose the ratio and give the reason (opposite and adjacent, so tan); (4) Calculate: height = (distance x tan angle) + 1.5 m, with units; (5) State the height as a sentence and explain why Wanjiru and Otieno agree. They then discuss the accuracy question: why 7.53 m and 7.51 m are not exactly 7.50 m and why Group Amani got 9.1 m instead of 9.0 m. They link this to angles read to the nearest degree. For example, learners test 15 x tan 26° + 1.5 and 15 x tan 28° + 1.5 using the calculator to see how a 1° change shifts the answer. Groups also explain in two or three sentences why the triangle size does not matter, using Lesson 2's idea that opposite ÷ adjacent depends only on the angle. Finally, groups briefly state why sin and cos would not be suitable for this problem (we know neither hypotenuse nor have a use for it), and that sin 53° would equal cos 37° as complementary angles. Each group presents to another group, and that group gives one 'glow' and one 'grow'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Imagine a Form One learner in Nakuru who missed our lessons. Your solution must let that learner find the tank height alone.' Display the five-step frame. Circulate and use probing questions: 'Why does your answer need the 1.5 m?' 'What does tan 37° = 0.7536 mean in words?' (For every 1 m along the ground, the line of sight rises 0.7536 m.) 'Why is the triangle at Otieno's position bigger but the same height answer?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 groups to explain the rounding error and take a total of 3 different explanations. Then run the 1° sensitivity test: ask half the class to compute 15 x tan 26° + 1.5 (8.3 m) and half 15 x tan 28° + 1.5 (9.5 m); with 15 x tan 27° + 1.5 = 9.1 m, ask 'What does a 1° slip do over 15 m?' Link: 'A flagpole 9.0 m is read at 9.1 m. Is the method wrong, or is the reading limited?' Press for the claim-evidence-reasoning structure: 'Claim: ___. Evidence: ___. Reasoning: ___.' Pose the connecting question: 'Surveyors on the Thika Superhighway and foresters in the Mau Forest use this idea. What stays the same, and what changes?' Cold-call 2 learners.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with a structured written solution frame. Learners must connect a claim (the tank is 7.5 m) to evidence (two sets of clinometer data and the tape check) and to the reasoning (the ratio depends only on the angle). The sensitivity test builds quantitative reasoning about measurement error, and gallery-style peer feedback improves clarity of explanations.
framework.formativeAssessment: Use a 4-point checklist for each group's solution: (a) labelled diagram, (b) triangle and ratio justified, (c) calculation with 1.5 m added and units, (d) explanation that the ratio depends on angle and not triangle size. Look for explanations that mention the nearest-degree reading limit, and for correct vocabulary (opposite, adjacent, elevation, tangent). Note learners who cannot explain why both learners get the same height, and re-teach through the Lesson 2 35° triangle table if needed.

framework.learnerExperience: The class returns to the Driving Question Board from Lesson 1, which has the columns 'Questions', 'Answered' and 'New understandings'. In groups, learners reread every question on the board and decide which can now be moved to 'Answered' (for example: 'How can we find the height without climbing?', 'What do sin, cos and tan mean?', 'Why do two learners get different angles?', 'How do we build a clinometer?'). For each moved question, they write the answer and a piece of evidence (such as the Lesson 2 table, the clinometer reading, or the Group Amani data) on a sticky note. They add 'New understandings' notes, such as 'The ratio opposite ÷ adjacent depends only on the angle', 'We must add eye height', and 'Reading to the nearest degree causes small errors'. They also add any remaining or new questions, such as 'How could we find an angle if we know two sides?', or 'What about triangles without a right angle?', which point to future learning.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our board started with wonderings. Let us see which ones we have earned the right to answer.' Read each question aloud and WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before groups decide. Ask: 'What evidence lets us move this one?' Cold-call 5 learners from different groups, each to defend moving one question using a specific lesson (for example: 'Lesson 5, our clinometer reading'). Challenge any answer without evidence: 'Can you show me where we saw that?' Identify any question not fully answered and treat it honestly: for example, 'Finding an angle from two sides is for a later lesson,' and mark it as a future question. Ask the final DQB question: 'Which question surprised you most by how well we can now answer it?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a record of conceptual change. Moving questions to 'Answered' with evidence makes the learning trail visible and links lessons together. Keeping unresolved questions respects authentic inquiry and shows that science and mathematics continue to generate new questions.
framework.formativeAssessment: Count how many questions each group moves with a specific evidence reference to a lesson. Check 'New understandings' for accuracy: ratio depends on angle only, add 1.5 m, nearest-degree error. Look for learners who cite evidence versus those who simply assert. Note which questions remain unresolved and whether they are reasonable extensions, not misunderstandings.

framework.learnerExperience: Individually, learners take out their Lesson 1 model, drawn before any instruction (usually a drawing of the tower and learners with a guess). They create a Final Model on a new page: a labelled diagram of the tank tower with Wanjiru at 8 m, 37°, Otieno at 10 m, 31°, the 1.5 m eye height, the horizontal at eye level, the right-angled triangle, the sides labelled opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse, and the equation height = (distance x tan angle) + 1.5 m. They add annotations: tan 37° = 0.7536 and tan 31° = 0.6009, both giving 7.5 m, and Mr. Kamau's tape check of 7.5 m. They then write their Final Explanation (6-8 sentences) answering: 'How can we use the angles and one side of a right-angled triangle to find any unknown height or distance in our environment, without ever measuring it directly?' and 'Why is trigonometry important?' They must include: the ratio idea, the choice of tan, the eye height, the consistency check, the rounding error, and at least one real-world use (surveyors in the Kenyan highlands, engineers on the Thika Superhighway, or foresters in the Mau Forest). Finally, learners place Lesson 1 and Final Models side by side and write three differences, then share with a partner.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Put your first model next to your final one. The difference is what you learned.' Give the Final Explanation checklist: ratio idea, tan chosen and why, eye height, consistency check, rounding error, real-world use. Circulate, and ask: 'What does your model show that your first one did not?' 'Where does your equation appear in the drawing?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 4 learners to read their Final Explanation aloud, and ask the class to listen for the checklist items. Ask 2 learners to compare Lesson 1 and Final models aloud. Close with: 'Wanjiru and Otieno stood in different places and saw different angles, yet the tank is one tank. Why is trigonometry important?' Take 3 responses, and affirm that the ratio opposite ÷ adjacent depends only on the angle, so a measured angle and a measured distance on the ground can replace a climb. Encourage learners to be proud: 'You have done what a surveyor does.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model comparison (Lesson 1 versus Final) and Final Explanation. Placing the early and final models side by side makes conceptual growth visible, and self-explanation consolidates learning. Writing against a checklist ensures that the explanation integrates side naming, ratios, calculation, error and real-world relevance.
framework.formativeAssessment: Score the Final Model and Explanation against the checklist: diagram labelled correctly; equation with 1.5 m; both learners' calculations leading to 7.5 m; ratio depends only on angle; rounding error explained; real-world application named. Success looks like a learner independently explaining why two different angles give one height. Exceeds: explains that a 1° reading error causes about 0.1 to 0.2 m difference at these distances. Approaching: leaves out eye height or cannot justify tan. Record these for follow-up and revision.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: (1) Could every learner draw a correctly labelled diagram, with the angle at the eye and the 1.5 m eye height shown separately, before calculating? Which learners still add or omit 1.5 m? (2) Did learners explain with confidence why Wanjiru (8 m, 37°) and Otieno (10 m, 31°) agree, using the idea that opposite ÷ adjacent depends only on the angle? (3) How well did learners handle the 0.1 m discrepancy between Group Amani's 9.1 m and the tape's 9.0 m, and the 7.53 m and 7.51 m against 7.5 m? FINAL_EXPLANATION.instructions: This is your Final Explanation. It answers the driving question: How can we use the angles and one side of a right-angled triangle to find any unknown height or distance in our environment, without ever measuring it directly? It also answers the key inquiry question: Why is trigonometry important? Write your answers in the space under each prompt. Use what you observed and learned in Lessons 1 to 8 and the Kilimani Secondary School water tank in Nakuru as your main example. Use a calculator in DEG mode. Give trig values to 4 decimal places and final lengths to 1 decimal place with units. Show every step of your working, draw labelled diagrams where asked, and use the words hypotenuse, opposite, adjacent, sin, cos and tan carefully.

sections.title: Part 1: The triangle and the ratio that makes the method work
sections.prompt: At Kilimani Secondary School nobody can climb the steel-framed water tank tower, but Wanjiru and Otieno can still find its height. (a) Draw and label the right-angled triangle formed by the tower, the level ground and the line of sight for Wanjiru, who stands 8 m from the base. Mark the angle θ at her eye, and label the hypotenuse, opposite and adjacent sides. Say what each side represents in the real situation. (b) Using the three 35° triangles A, B and C from Lesson 2 (sides 4.0, 2.8, 4.9 cm; 8.0, 5.6, 9.8 cm; 12.0, 8.4, 14.7 cm), explain what you found about the ratios when the triangles got bigger. (c) Explain why this idea matters for the tank.
sections.exemplar:
(a) The diagram is a right-angled triangle. Its horizontal side runs from Wanjiru's eye, level with her eye height, to the tower. Its vertical side is the part of the tower above her eye level. The right angle is where the horizontal line from her eye meets the tower. The line of sight from her eye to the top of the tank is the hypotenuse, which is opposite the right angle and is the longest side. The angle θ is at her eye, between the horizontal and the line of sight. The opposite side is the part of the tower above her eye level, which is across from θ. The adjacent side is the 8 m horizontal distance from her to the tower, next to θ and not the hypotenuse.
(b) Triangles A, B and C all have a 35° angle but different sizes. In every one, opposite ÷ hypotenuse was about 0.571, adjacent ÷ hypotenuse was about 0.816 and opposite ÷ adjacent was about 0.700. These are sin 35°, cos 35° and tan 35°, and the calculator gives 0.5736, 0.8192 and 0.7002, very close to our measurements. The ratios stayed the same even though the triangles got bigger, apart from small measuring differences of about 0.02.
(c) For a fixed angle, the ratio of the sides depends only on the angle, not on the size of the triangle. So Wanjiru's small triangle and Otieno's bigger triangle at different distances can give the same height. Knowing the angle and one side lets us find another side, so we do not need to measure the height directly.

sections.title: Part 2: Choosing a ratio and calculating
sections.prompt: (a) Explain how you decide whether to use sin, cos or tan when you need to find an unknown side. (b) Use the 3-step method (label, choose the ratio, solve with units) to find: (i) the length of a Kisumu roof rafter when the horizontal span from the wall to the centre is 3.6 m and the rafter makes 30° with the horizontal; (ii) the width of a Kericho stream, when a learner on the bank directly opposite a tree walks 20 m along the bank and the line of sight to the tree then makes 40° with the bank. (c) A Watamu diver's weighted line is 12 m long and makes 50° with the horizontal surface. Find the depth of the weight.
sections.exemplar:
(a) I label the triangle from the angle θ and identify the side I know and the side I want. If they are opposite and adjacent I use tan. If they are opposite and hypotenuse I use sin. If they are adjacent and hypotenuse I use cos. Then I write the equation, solve it and give the answer with units.
(b)(i) The known side is the adjacent side (3.6 m) and the wanted side is the hypotenuse (the rafter), so I use cos. cos 30° = 3.6 ÷ rafter, so rafter = 3.6 ÷ cos 30° = 3.6 ÷ 0.8660 = 4.2 m.
(ii) The known side is the 20 m walked along the bank (adjacent) and the wanted side is the stream width (opposite), so I use tan. Width = 20 × tan 40° = 20 × 0.8391 = 16.8 m.
(c) The known side is the line, 12 m, which is the hypotenuse, and the wanted side is the depth, which is opposite the 50° angle. So I use sin. Depth = 12 × sin 50° = 12 × 0.7660 = 9.2 m.

sections.title: Part 3: Solving the water tank problem
sections.prompt: Wanjiru stands 8 m from the base of the tower and reads an angle of elevation of 37°. Otieno stands 10 m from the base and reads 31°. Every learner's eye height is 1.5 m. (a) Explain how the clinometer gives the angle of elevation, and what the string does when the straw is level. (b) Write a complete solution for Wanjiru: the diagram description, the ratio and why you chose it, the calculation and the answer with units. (c) Do the same for Otieno. (d) Wanjiru is closer, so whose angle is larger? Explain why both learners should still get the same height.
sections.exemplar:
(a) The clinometer is a cardboard protractor with a straw along the straight edge and a string with a washer hanging from the centre mark. When the straw is level the string hangs at the 90° mark. When the straw is tilted up to sight the top of the tank, the string moves away from 90°. The angle of elevation is the number of degrees between the string and the 90° mark.
(b) The tower, the level ground and the line of sight form a right-angled triangle. The known side is the 8 m horizontal distance (adjacent) and the wanted side is the height above eye level (opposite), so I use tan. Height above eye level = 8 × tan 37° = 8 × 0.7536 = 6.03 m. Adding the 1.5 m eye height: 6.03 + 1.5 = 7.53 m, which is 7.5 m to 1 d.p.
(c) The same triangle shape, with adjacent = 10 m and θ = 31°, so I use tan. Height above eye level = 10 × tan 31° = 10 × 0.6009 = 6.01 m. Adding 1.5 m: 6.01 + 1.5 = 7.51 m, which is 7.5 m.
(d) Wanjiru is closer (8 m), so she has the larger angle (37° compared with 31°). Both get 7.5 m because tan is the ratio opposite ÷ adjacent, which depends only on the angle, so height above eye level = distance × tan(angle) for each learner. Both learners are measuring the same tower, so each pair of distance and angle gives the same height above eye level, 6.0 m, and the same total height.

sections.title: Part 4: Checking the answer and sources of error
sections.prompt: Group Amani used their clinometers on the school flagpole, standing 15 m from the base and reading 27°. Mr. Kamau, the school caretaker, used a tape to check the heights: the flagpole is 9.0 m and the top of the water tank is 7.5 m. (a) Calculate Group Amani's flagpole height. (b) Work out their error. (c) Explain why small differences like this happen. (d) Use your answers from Part 3 and Mr. Kamau's tape value for the tank to judge whether Wanjiru's and Otieno's answers are good.
sections.exemplar:
(a) The known side is the 15 m horizontal distance (adjacent) and the wanted side is the height above eye level (opposite), so I use tan. Height = 15 × tan 27° + 1.5 = 15 × 0.5095 + 1.5 = 7.64 + 1.5 = 9.14 m, which is 9.1 m to 1 d.p.
(b) The error is 9.14 − 9.0 = 0.14 m, about 0.1 m when the heights are given to 1 d.p. (9.1 − 9.0).
(c) The angle is read from the clinometer to the nearest degree, so it can be up to half a degree out. Small differences in where the string rests, the straw not being held perfectly steady, and distances measured along the ground also add small errors. Because the angle is rounded, the calculated height is close to the real height but not exact.
(d) Mr. Kamau's tape value for the top of the tank is 7.5 m. Wanjiru's answer (7.53 m) and Otieno's answer (7.51 m) both round to 7.5 m, so they agree with the tape within the rounding error from reading angles to the nearest degree. This shows the method works.

sections.title: Part 5: Answering the driving question
sections.prompt: Write a clear explanation in your own words that answers: How can we use the angles and one side of a right-angled triangle to find an unknown height or distance in our environment, without measuring it directly? Use the Kilimani Secondary School water tank as your example. Include: the triangle, why the method works, the steps, and how you know the answer can be trusted. Then answer the key inquiry question: Why is trigonometry important? Give at least two real-life Kenyan examples.
sections.exemplar:
We can find the height of the tank without climbing it because the tower, the level ground and the line of sight form a right-angled triangle. We measure the horizontal distance along level ground with a tape and the angle of elevation with a clinometer. For a given angle, the ratio opposite ÷ adjacent (tan) is the same whatever the size of the triangle. That is why tan of the angle links the distance to the height above eye level: height above eye level = distance × tan(angle). For Wanjiru, 8 × tan 37° = 6.03 m, and adding the 1.5 m eye height gives 7.5 m. For Otieno, 10 × tan 31° = 6.01 m, and adding 1.5 m also gives 7.5 m. They stand at different distances and read different angles, but they agree because both are measuring the same tower and the ratio depends only on the angle. To solve any problem I label the triangle, choose sin, cos or tan from the known and wanted sides, calculate in DEG mode, add the eye height when needed, and state the answer with units. I can trust the answer because both learners agree and because Mr. Kamau's tape check of 7.5 m matches within the small error from reading angles to the nearest degree, as with the flagpole where we got 9.1 m against 9.0 m.
Trigonometry is important because it lets us find heights and distances that are too difficult, too dangerous or impossible to measure directly. Surveyors use it to map the Kenyan highlands, engineers use it to design the Thika Superhighway overpasses, and foresters use it to measure tree heights in the Mau Forest without felling the trees. It is also used by a Rift Valley farmer to estimate the height of a cliff, or by builders to find the length of a Kisumu roof rafter.

SUMMARY_TABLE.drivingQuestion: DRIVING QUESTION: How can we use the angles and one side of a right-angled triangle to find any unknown height or distance in our environment — without ever measuring it directly?

lessons.title: The Water Tank Problem: Predict and Name the Sides
lessons.observed: We observed that the water tank tower at Kilimani Secondary School cannot be climbed, yet Wanjiru and Otieno stand at different distances from its base and sight the top of the tank to record different angles. The tower, the ground and the line of sight form a right-angled triangle.
lessons.learned: We learned to name the sides of a right-angled triangle relative to a chosen acute angle θ: the hypotenuse is opposite the right angle and is the longest side; the opposite side is across from θ; the adjacent side is next to θ but is not the hypotenuse. When θ moves to the other acute angle, opposite and adjacent swap but the hypotenuse stays the same.
lessons.explained: We can say that the height of the tank above eye level is the opposite side and the distance from the learner to the tower is the adjacent side for the angle at the learner's eye, but we cannot yet explain how the angle and distance give the height, or whether Wanjiru and Otieno should get the same answer. These questions are on our Driving Question Board and we will answer them in the next lessons.

lessons.title: Deriving sine, cosine and tangent: Why does the tank method work at any distance?
lessons.observed: What did you measure and calculate for the three 35° triangles A, B and C? Record the adjacent, opposite and hypotenuse lengths, and the three ratios (opposite ÷ hypotenuse, adjacent ÷ hypotenuse, opposite ÷ adjacent) for each triangle. What did you notice about the ratios as the triangles got bigger?
lessons.learned: What are sin θ, cos θ and tan θ in terms of opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse? What are the calculator values of sin 35°, cos 35° and tan 35° in DEG mode, and how close are they to your measured ratios?
lessons.explained: Why do the ratios stay the same for triangles of different sizes with the same angle? How does this idea help explain how Wanjiru (8 m, 37°) and Otieno (10 m, 31°) at Kilimani Secondary School can both find the same tank height without climbing the tower? What do you still need to learn to calculate that height?

lessons.title: Complementary Angles: Why Does sin 20° Equal cos 70°?
lessons.observed: Complete the Lesson 3 table. For the pairs 20°/70°, 30°/60°, 35°/55° and 45°/45°, we found that sin of one angle equals cos of the other (for example sin 20° = cos 70° = 0.3420 and sin 35° = cos 55° = 0.5736). At 45° the sine and cosine are equal (0.7071).
lessons.learned: Two acute angles in a right-angled triangle add up to 90° and are called complementary. The side opposite one angle is the side adjacent to the other. So sin θ = cos(90° - θ) and cos θ = sin(90° - θ). Wanjiru's 37° at the tank goes with 53° at the top of her line of sight.
lessons.explained: Write in your own words why sin 35° = cos 55°, using the words opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse, and say how this helps us get closer to finding the height of the Kilimani Secondary School water tank without climbing it.

lessons.title: Choosing the Right Ratio: Solving for Unknown Sides and the First Full Tank-Height Calculation
lessons.observed: We observed that to find an unknown side, we label the triangle from the angle, pick the ratio that links the KNOWN side and the WANTED side, write the equation and solve. In the tank problem, Wanjiru is 8 m away at 37 degrees, so 8 x tan 37 = 6.03 m above eye level, and with her 1.5 m eye height the top of the tank is 7.5 m.
lessons.learned: We learned that tan links opposite and adjacent, sin links opposite and hypotenuse, and cos links adjacent and hypotenuse. We learned that the ratio depends only on the angle, so one angle and one side are enough to find another side. We also learned to use tan 37 = 0.7536 in DEG mode and to add the 1.5 m eye height.
lessons.explained: We can now partly explain how the tank height can be found without climbing it: the known distance and the angle give a ratio that lets us calculate the height. We still need to explain how to measure the angle accurately, and to check that Otieno (10 m, 31 degrees) gets the same height, which we will test in later lessons.

lessons.title: Angle of Elevation and Building the Clinometer
lessons.observed: We built a clinometer from a cardboard protractor, a straw, a string and a washer. When the straw is level the string hangs at the 90° mark, and when we sighted the top of the classroom door frame (2.1 m high) from 3.0 m the string moved away from 90° by about 11°.
lessons.learned: The angle of elevation is the angle above the horizontal from the observer's eye up to the object. On the clinometer it is the number of degrees between the string and the 90° mark, so the scale reading is 90° minus the angle of elevation (complementary angles). Height = (distance × tan angle) + 1.5 m.
lessons.explained: Wanjiru can get an angle for the Kilimani Secondary School water tank without climbing because her clinometer measures the angle of elevation from her eye. That angle, together with her 8 m horizontal distance, gives a right-angled triangle in which tan connects the two, and adding her 1.5 m eye height gives the tank's height.
